highlights.LOF2011: Last author of the study showing that ULK1 phosphorylates AMPK in a negative feedback loop.

Dan L.lab_name: Antibiotics Innovation and Resistance Control Key Laboratory of Sichuan Province, School of Pharmacy, Chengdu University (Chengdu, China)
Dan L.role: First author of a 2026 fission yeast study of resistance to TORC1 inhibitors.
Dan L.sub: School of Pharmacy · Chengdu University · Chengdu, China
story: Lufeng Dan is first author of a 2026 paper in Microbiology Spectrum. In fission yeast, resistance to rapamycin plus caffeine came and went from one generation to the next. The team found that this was not an epigenetic switch. Instead, loss-of-function mutations in the gaf1 gene appeared under drug pressure and reverted to the normal sequence when resistance was lost. Gaf1 encodes a GATA transcription factor that slows growth downstream of TORC1. PubMed lists him at the School of Pharmacy, Chengdu University.

highlights.DAN2026: First author of the yeast study tracing reversible TORC1 inhibitor resistance to gaf1 mutations.

Demidenko ZN.role: First author of the 2009 Cell Cycle study showing that rapamycin slows cellular senescence.
story: Zoya N Demidenko is first author of a 2009 paper in Cell Cycle. In human and rodent cell lines, the team blocked the cell cycle and let cell growth continue, which pushed cells into permanent senescence. Rapamycin kept the arrested cells able to start dividing again once the block was removed. This is evidence that mTOR helps drive the senescent state. PubMed lists her only at Oncotarget in Albany, New York.

highlights.DEM2009: First author of the cell-line study showing that rapamycin decelerates cellular senescence.

Demir A.role: First author of a 2026 Blood study on IDH3, citrate and venetoclax resistance in acute myeloid leukemia.
story: Aykut Demir is first author of a 2026 paper in Blood. The work covers leukemic stem cells from acute myeloid leukemia, studied in cells, organoids and mice. Losing IDH3A, an enzyme of the TCA cycle, raised citrate and caused an energy crisis. That activated AMPK and lowered mTORC1 activity and protein production, which made the cells more sensitive to the drug venetoclax. PubMed lists him at Heidelberg University.

highlights.DEM2026: First author of the study linking IDH3A, citrate, AMPK and mTORC1 to venetoclax sensitivity in AML stem cells.

Zamboni N.lab_name: Institute of Molecular Systems Biology, ETH Zurich (Zurich, Switzerland)
Zamboni N.role: Co-author of two Atlas studies, a 2016 T cell arginine study and a 2026 leukemia metabolism study.
Zamboni N.sub: Institute of Molecular Systems Biology · ETH Zurich · Zurich, Switzerland
story: Nicola Zamboni is a middle author on two Atlas studies. The 2016 Cell paper followed metabolites and proteins in activated human T cells, in cells and a mouse model. It found that raising L-arginine moved the cells toward oxidative metabolism and gave them longer survival.

The 2026 Blood paper found that losing IDH3A in leukemic stem cells raises citrate, activates AMPK and lowers mTORC1 activity. PubMed lists him at the Institute of Molecular Systems Biology at ETH Zurich in both papers.

highlights.GEI2016: Middle author of the study on L-arginine, T cell metabolism and anti-tumor activity.
highlights.DEM2026: Middle author of the study on IDH3, citrate and venetoclax resistance in AML stem cells.

Demmings MD.lab_name: Neuroscience Program and Robarts Research Institute, University of Western Ontario (London, Ontario, Canada)
Demmings MD.role: First author of a 2026 Cell Reports study on ATF4, mTOR suppression and neuron loss in Parkinson disease models.
Demmings MD.sub: Neuroscience Program & Robarts Research Institute · University of Western Ontario · London, ON, Canada
story: Matthew D Demmings is first author of a 2026 paper in Cell Reports. In cell and animal models of Parkinson disease, long-lasting stress signaling through ATF4 turned up SESN2, DDIT4 and Trib3. Together these lowered both mTORC1 and mTORC2 activity, and that loss of mTOR signaling helped kill dopamine neurons through the protein PUMA. This is a case where too little mTOR activity is harmful. PubMed lists him at the University of Western Ontario.

highlights.DEMMINGS2026: First author of the study linking ATF4-driven mTOR suppression to dopaminergic neuron death in Parkinson disease models.

De Nardi A.lab_name: Centre for Computational and Systems Biology (COSBI), Fondazione The Microsoft Research - University of Trento (Rovereto, Italy)
De Nardi A.role: First author of a 2026 survival analysis of the RAP-ALS rapamycin trial.
De Nardi A.sub: COSBI · Fondazione The Microsoft Research - University of Trento · Rovereto, Italy
story: Alex De Nardi is first author of a 2026 paper in the European Journal of Neurology. It is a secondary, retrospective analysis of data from RAP-ALS, a rapamycin trial in 63 people with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis. The authors saw longer survival in the few treated people who carry a C9orf72 mutation. They call this exploratory because the group was small. PubMed lists him at COSBI in Rovereto and the Department of Mathematics at the University of Trento.

highlights.DEN2026B: First author of the exploratory survival analysis of the RAP-ALS rapamycin trial.

de Oliveira Isídio BE.lab_name: Department of Genetics, Federal University of Pernambuco (Recife, Brazil)
de Oliveira Isídio BE.role: First author of a 2026 study of HPV16 oncogene expression and PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathway genes in breast tumors.
de Oliveira Isídio BE.sub: Department of Genetics · Federal University of Pernambuco · Recife, Brazil
story: Beatriz Eda de Oliveira Isídio is first author of a 2026 paper in Exploration of Targeted Anti-Tumor Therapy. The team measured RNA in breast tumor tissue from 48 of 92 patients. Samples with HPV16 oncogene expression had higher PI3K and lower mTOR transcript levels. The study only compares mRNA levels, so it does not show that the virus switches on the mTOR pathway. PubMed lists her at the Federal University of Pernambuco.

highlights.DEOLIVEIRA2026: First author of the study of HPV16 oncogenes and PI3K/AKT/mTOR transcripts in breast tumors.

Dibbens LM.lab_name: Epilepsy Research Program, School of Pharmacy and Medical Sciences, University of South Australia (Adelaide, South Australia, Australia)
Dibbens LM.role: First author of the 2013 Nature Genetics study linking DEPDC5 mutations to familial focal epilepsy.
Dibbens LM.sub: Epilepsy Research Program · University of South Australia · Adelaide, Australia
story: Leanne M Dibbens is first author of a 2013 paper in Nature Genetics. Using exome sequencing in families with focal epilepsy, the team found loss-of-function mutations in DEPDC5, which codes for a part of the GATOR1 complex. They found these mutations in 5 of 6 further published large families and in about 12% (10 of 82) of smaller families. This is human genetic evidence that GATOR1 matters for brain function. PubMed lists her at the University of South Australia.

highlights.DIB2013B: First author of the study that found DEPDC5 mutations in familial focal epilepsy.

Dorrello NV.lab_name: Department of Pathology, NYU Cancer Institute, New York University School of Medicine (New York, New York, USA)
Dorrello NV.role: First author of the 2006 Science study on S6K1 and the degradation of PDCD4.
Dorrello NV.sub: Department of Pathology, NYU Cancer Institute · New York University School of Medicine · New York, NY, USA
story: N Valerio Dorrello is first author of a 2006 paper in Science. In cultured cells, the kinase S6K1 phosphorylates the tumor suppressor PDCD4, and the ubiquitin ligase betaTRCP then marks it for destruction. Losing PDCD4 lets translation and cell growth go ahead. PubMed lists him at the Department of Pathology, NYU Cancer Institute, New York University School of Medicine.

highlights.DOR2006: First author of the study showing that S6K1 and betaTRCP degrade PDCD4 to promote translation.

Drummond MJ.lab_name: Department of Physical Therapy, University of Texas Medical Branch (Galveston, Texas, USA)
Drummond MJ.role: First author of the 2009 human study of rapamycin and muscle protein synthesis after exercise.
Drummond MJ.sub: Department of Physical Therapy · University of Texas Medical Branch · Galveston, TX, USA
story: Micah J Drummond is first author of a 2009 paper in The Journal of Physiology. Healthy volunteers took rapamycin before a bout of resistance exercise. The usual rise of about 40% in muscle protein synthesis in the first one to two hours was blocked. The study measured short-term protein synthesis, not muscle growth. PubMed lists him at the Department of Physical Therapy, University of Texas Medical Branch.

highlights.DRU2009: First author of the human study showing that rapamycin blocks the exercise-induced rise in muscle protein synthesis.

Duran RV.role: First author of the 2012 Molecular Cell study on glutaminolysis and Rag-mTORC1 signaling.
Duran RV.sub: Biozentrum · University of Basel · Basel, Switzerland
story: Raúl V Durán is first author of a 2012 paper in Molecular Cell. In cultured cells, glutamine together with leucine switched on mTORC1 by raising the production of alpha-ketoglutarate through glutaminolysis. This worked upstream of the Rag GTPases. PubMed lists him at the Biozentrum, University of Basel.

highlights.DUR2012: First author of the study showing that glutaminolysis activates Rag-mTORC1 signaling.

Robitaille AM.role: First author of the 2013 Science phosphoproteomics study showing that mTORC1 activates pyrimidine synthesis.
Robitaille AM.sub: Biozentrum · University of Basel · Basel, Switzerland
story: Aaron M Robitaille is first author of a 2013 paper in Science. Using quantitative phosphoproteomics in cells, the team found that mTOR controls the phosphorylation of 335 proteins. One of them, CAD, runs the first steps of making pyrimidines, the building blocks of DNA and RNA. mTORC1 acts through S6 kinase to switch CAD on. PubMed lists him at the Biozentrum, University of Basel.

highlights.ROB2013: First author of the study showing that mTORC1 activates de novo pyrimidine synthesis.

Duran-Ortiz S.lab_name: Institute for Molecular Medicine and Aging, Heritage College of Osteopathic Medicine, Ohio University (Athens, Ohio, USA)
Duran-Ortiz S.role: First author of a 2026 Aging Cell study of growth hormone receptor deletion in middle-aged mice.
Duran-Ortiz S.sub: Institute for Molecular Medicine and Aging · Ohio University · Athens, OH, USA
story: Silvana Duran-Ortiz is first author of a 2026 paper in Aging Cell. In mice, deleting the growth hormone receptor at 12 months of age still extended lifespan in both sexes, without big effects on body size. Males also kept better insulin sensitivity, muscle performance and bone structure with age. The work is in mice, not people. PubMed lists her at the Institute for Molecular Medicine and Aging, Ohio University.

highlights.DUR2026: First author of the mouse study of growth hormone receptor deletion at 12 months of age.

Ikeno Y.lab_name: Sam and Ann Barshop Institute for Longevity and Aging Studies, University of Texas Health Science Center at San Antonio (San Antonio, Texas, USA)
Ikeno Y.role: Co-author of two Atlas studies, one on rapamycin and senescent cells and one on growth hormone receptor deletion in mice.
Ikeno Y.sub: Barshop Institute for Longevity and Aging Studies · UT Health San Antonio · San Antonio, TX, USA
story: Yuji Ikeno is a middle author on two Atlas studies. The 2015 Nature Cell Biology paper found that rapamycin lowers the inflammatory signals of senescent cells by cutting the translation of IL1A, and that it reduced the ability of senescent cells to help prostate tumors grow in mice.

The 2026 Aging Cell paper found that deleting the growth hormone receptor in middle-aged mice extended lifespan. PubMed lists him at the Barshop Institute for Longevity and Aging Studies in San Antonio in both papers.

highlights.LAB2015: Middle author of the study showing that mTOR drives the senescence-associated secretory phenotype through IL1A translation.
highlights.DUR2026: Middle author of the mouse study of growth hormone receptor deletion at 12 months of age.

Evans S.lab_name: Department of Integrative Neuroscience, Guarini School of Graduate and Advanced Studies, Dartmouth College (Hanover, New Hampshire, USA)
Evans S.role: First author of a 2026 eNeuro study on PTEN, mTORC2 and microtubules in sensory neurons.
Evans S.sub: Department of Integrative Neuroscience · Dartmouth College · Hanover, NH, USA
story: Simone Evans is first author of a 2026 paper in eNeuro. In mouse sensory neurons without Pten, the team removed Raptor (mTORC1) or Rictor (mTORC2) to see which complex drives faster microtubule growth and larger neurons. Removing mTORC2, but not mTORC1, brought these features back to normal, and the effect was in the growth cone at the axon tip. PubMed lists her at the Department of Integrative Neuroscience, Dartmouth College.

highlights.EVA2026: First author of the study showing that PTEN acts through mTORC2, not mTORC1, on microtubule polymerization.

Fan W.lab_name: Department of Radiation Oncology and Molecular Radiation Sciences, Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine (Baltimore, Maryland, USA)
Fan W.role: First author of a 2026 Genes & Development study on mTOR inactivation and ribosome biogenesis deficiency.
Fan W.sub: Department of Radiation Oncology and Molecular Radiation Sciences · Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine · Baltimore, MD, USA
story: Wenjun Fan is first author of a 2026 paper in Genes & Development. When ribosome production is impaired, mTORC1 inhibition does not restore it. Instead it moves the limited ribosomes away from highly translated 5'TOP mRNAs and toward mRNAs that cells need to survive. The authors call this translational fitness. PubMed lists her at Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine and the University of Maryland School of Medicine.

highlights.FAN2026: First author of the study on mTOR inactivation and adaptive survival under ribosome biogenesis deficiency.

Feldman ME.lab_name: Department of Cellular and Molecular Pharmacology, University of California San Francisco (San Francisco, California, USA)
Feldman ME.role: First author of the 2009 PLoS Biology study of active-site mTOR inhibitors (TORKinibs).
Feldman ME.sub: Howard Hughes Medical Institute & Department of Cellular and Molecular Pharmacology · University of California San Francisco · San Francisco, CA, USA
story: Morris E Feldman is first author of a 2009 paper in PLoS Biology. The team made two mTOR kinase-domain inhibitors, PP242 and PP30, and tested them in cells and animals. Unlike rapamycin they block mTORC2 as well, and PP242 shut down cap-dependent translation that rapamycin left running. PubMed lists him at the Howard Hughes Medical Institute and the Department of Cellular and Molecular Pharmacology, University of California San Francisco.

highlights.FEL2009: First author of the study introducing the TORKinibs PP242 and PP30.

Flynn JM.lab_name: Buck Institute for Research on Aging (Novato, California, USA)
Flynn JM.role: First author of the 2013 Aging Cell study of late-life rapamycin and heart function in mice.
Flynn JM.sub: Buck Institute for Research on Aging · Novato, CA, USA
story: James M Flynn is first author of a 2013 paper in Aging Cell. Female mice aged 24 months were given rapamycin for 3 months. Their hearts showed reversal or reduction of several age-related changes in function. RNA sequencing suggested effects on inflammation, metabolism and heart growth. The work is in mice. PubMed lists him at the Buck Institute for Research on Aging.

highlights.FLY2013: First author of the mouse study showing that late-life rapamycin reverses age-related heart dysfunction.

Diaz V.lab_name: Department of Cellular and Integrative Physiology, Barshop Institute for Longevity and Aging Studies, University of Texas Health Science Center at San Antonio (San Antonio, Texas, USA)
Diaz V.role: Co-author of two Atlas mouse lifespan studies on rapamycin.
Diaz V.sub: Barshop Institute for Longevity and Aging Studies · UT Health San Antonio · San Antonio, TX, USA
story: Vivian Diaz is a middle author on two Atlas studies. The 2014 PLoS One paper found that rapamycin-fed mice lived longer and showed large changes in the liver transcriptome, more in females than in males.

The 2022 Aging Cell paper reported lifespan results from the NIA Interventions Testing Program, where rapamycin plus acarbose lengthened life in male mice more than rapamycin alone did in earlier cohorts. PubMed lists her at the Barshop Institute for Longevity and Aging Studies in both papers.

highlights.FOK2014: Middle author of the mouse study of rapamycin, lifespan and the liver transcriptome.
highlights.STR2022: Middle author of the Interventions Testing Program study of rapamycin plus acarbose and captopril.

Fok WC.lab_name: Department of Cellular and Structural Biology, University of Texas Health Science Center at San Antonio (San Antonio, Texas, USA)
Fok WC.role: First author of the 2014 PLoS One study of rapamycin, lifespan and the liver transcriptome in mice.
Fok WC.sub: Department of Cellular and Structural Biology · UT Health San Antonio · San Antonio, TX, USA
story: Wilson C Fok is first author of a 2014 paper in PLoS One. Mice fed rapamycin from 4 months of age lived 11% to 16% longer. The team compared liver gene activity at 25 months and found over 4,500 changed transcripts in females but far fewer in most males. Mitochondrial function was the most changed pathway. PubMed lists him at the Department of Cellular and Structural Biology, University of Texas Health Science Center at San Antonio.

highlights.FOK2014: First author of the mouse study of rapamycin, lifespan and the liver transcriptome.

Foretz M.lab_name: Institut Cochin, Université Paris Descartes, CNRS (Paris, France)
Foretz M.role: First author of the 2010 Journal of Clinical Investigation study of metformin and liver glucose production in mice.
Foretz M.sub: Institut Cochin · Université Paris Descartes, CNRS · Paris, France
story: Marc Foretz is first author of a 2010 paper in The Journal of Clinical Investigation. In mice and liver cells lacking AMPK or LKB1, metformin still lowered glucose production. The team linked the effect to a drop in the liver's energy state, so metformin does not need AMPK for this action. PubMed lists him at the Institut Cochin in Paris.

highlights.FOR2010: First author of the study showing that metformin suppresses liver gluconeogenesis without AMPK or LKB1.

Curatolo P.role: Co-author of the EXIST-3 trial of everolimus for seizures in tuberous sclerosis complex.
Curatolo P.sub: Tor Vergata University Hospital · Rome, Italy
story: The EXIST-3 trial gave everolimus or placebo to 366 people with tuberous sclerosis complex whose focal seizures had not responded to standard drugs. According to PubMed, about 15% of the placebo group had their seizures cut by half or more, against 28% on low-dose and 40% on high-dose everolimus. This was a randomised, double-blind trial in people.

Paolo Curatolo is a middle author on the paper, and PubMed lists him at Tor Vergata University Hospital in Rome. The Atlas also has him as a middle author of a second tuberous sclerosis trial, but that record gives no affiliation, so it is not included here.

highlights.FRE2016: Middle author of the phase 3 EXIST-3 trial, listed at Tor Vergata University Hospital, Rome.

Frias MA.lab_name: Whitehead Institute for Biomedical Research and Department of Biology, Massachusetts Institute of Technology (Cambridge, MA, USA)
Frias MA.role: First author of a 2006 cell study that identified mSin1 as part of mTORC2.
Frias MA.sub: Whitehead Institute for Biomedical Research & Department of Biology, MIT · Cambridge, MA, USA
story: This study in human cells found that a protein called mSin1 is needed for mTORC2 to be built and to switch on the kinase Akt. The mSin1 gene makes several versions of the protein, and three of them end up in distinct forms of mTORC2.
Maria Frias is first author. PubMed lists her at the Whitehead Institute and the Department of Biology at MIT.

highlights.FRI2006: First author of the paper showing mSin1 is required for mTORC2 assembly and Akt phosphorylation.

Xu C.lab_name: Department of Hematology, The Seventh Affiliated Hospital, Sun Yat-Sen University (Shenzhen, China)
Xu C.role: Last author of a 2026 study on a small tRNA fragment and drug resistance in multiple myeloma.
Xu C.sub: Department of Hematology, The Seventh Affiliated Hospital, Sun Yat-Sen University · Shenzhen, China
story: This 2026 study, done in myeloma cells and in mice, found that a small RNA fragment called tRF-17-8SPOL52 is high in relapsed or treatment-resistant myeloma. It makes the cells resistant to the drug bortezomib by switching off RUBCN, a brake on autophagy, so that autophagy runs more.
Cong Xu is the last author. PubMed lists him at the Department of Hematology of the Seventh Affiliated Hospital of Sun Yat-Sen University in Shenzhen.

highlights.FU2026: Last author and corresponding contact of the myeloma study, listed in Shenzhen.

Gan X.lab_name: Department of Pharmacology, Yale University School of Medicine (New Haven, CT, USA)
Gan X.role: First author of a 2011 cell study on how PIP3 activates mTORC2.
Gan X.sub: Department of Pharmacology, Yale University School of Medicine · New Haven, CT, USA
story: Working in cultured cells and in test-tube kinase assays, this study showed that the lipid PIP3 can directly boost the activity of mTORC2, the complex that switches on Akt. That links the PI3K pathway to mTORC2.
Xiaoqing Gan is first author. PubMed lists her at the Department of Pharmacology at Yale University School of Medicine.

highlights.GAN2011: First author of the study showing PIP3 directly stimulates mTORC2 kinase activity.

Gao X.lab_name: Department of Physiology, University of Texas Southwestern Medical Center at Dallas (Dallas, TX, USA)
Gao X.role: First author of a 2002 study showing that Tsc1 and Tsc2 work upstream of TOR.
Gao X.sub: Department of Physiology, University of Texas Southwestern Medical Center at Dallas · Dallas, TX, USA
story: This 2002 study used fruit flies and mammalian cells. It showed that the tumour suppressors Tsc1 and Tsc2 can bind TOR and act upstream of it. Cells missing Tsc1 or Tsc2 had more S6K activity, which depended on TOR, and they no longer switched S6K off when starved of amino acids.

Xinsheng Gao is first author. PubMed lists him at the Department of Physiology, UT Southwestern in Dallas. The Atlas has a second record under this name, but it carries no affiliation, so it is left out.

highlights.GAO2002: First author of the paper placing Tsc1 and Tsc2 upstream of TOR in amino-acid signalling.

Gao K.lab_name: Department of Urology, Xi'an People's Hospital (Xi'an Fourth Hospital), School of Medicine, Northwest University (Xi'an, China)
Gao K.role: First author of a 2026 multicenter study of everolimus in TSC-associated kidney angiomyolipomas.
Gao K.sub: Department of Urology, Xi'an People's Hospital (Xi'an Fourth Hospital), Northwest University · Xi'an, China
story: This prospective cohort study followed 183 people in China with kidney tumours (angiomyolipomas) from tuberous sclerosis complex. Everolimus shrank the tumours by half or more in 44% of patients at 3 months and 83% at 6 months, and fat-poor tumours responded better than fat-rich ones. A smaller dose looked similar in an exploratory, non-randomised comparison, so that point needs a randomised trial.
Ke Gao is first author. PubMed lists him in the Department of Urology at Xi'an People's Hospital.

highlights.GAO2026B: First author of the multicenter cohort study.

Ni J.lab_name: Department of Urology, Xi'an People's Hospital (Xi'an Fourth Hospital), School of Medicine, Northwest University (Xi'an, China)
Ni J.role: Last author of a 2026 multicenter study of everolimus in TSC-associated kidney angiomyolipomas.
Ni J.sub: Department of Urology, Xi'an People's Hospital (Xi'an Fourth Hospital), Northwest University · Xi'an, China
story: This prospective cohort study followed 183 people in China with kidney tumours (angiomyolipomas) from tuberous sclerosis complex. Everolimus shrank the tumours by half or more in 44% of patients at 3 months and 83% at 6 months, and fat-poor tumours responded better than fat-rich ones. The low-dose comparison was exploratory and not randomised.
Jianxin Ni is the last author. PubMed lists him in the Department of Urology at Xi'an People's Hospital.

highlights.GAO2026B: Last author of the multicenter cohort study.

Garami A.lab_name: Friedrich Miescher Institute for Biomedical Research (Basel, Switzerland)
Garami A.role: First author of a 2003 study showing that TSC1/2 acts on Rheb to control mTOR signalling.
Garami A.sub: Friedrich Miescher Institute for Biomedical Research · Basel, Switzerland
story: This 2003 cell study found that insulin switches on the small GTPase Rheb, and that the TSC1/TSC2 complex turns Rheb off by acting as its GAP (an enzyme that makes it hydrolyse GTP). Active Rheb then drives S6K1 signalling. This placed Rheb as a direct step upstream of mTOR.
Attila Garami is first author. PubMed lists him at the Friedrich Miescher Institute in Basel.

highlights.GAR2003: First author of the Rheb and TSC1/2 paper.

Stocker H.role: First author of a 2003 fruit-fly study showing Rheb is needed for S6K-driven cell growth.
Stocker H.sub: Zoologisches Institut der Universität Zürich · Zurich, Switzerland
story: In fruit flies, mutations in the Rheb gene stopped cell growth, while extra Rheb made cells grow more. The genetic and biochemical tests put Rheb downstream of Tsc1-Tsc2 in the TOR pathway, with S6K as a main effector.

Hugo Stocker is first author. PubMed lists him at the Zoological Institute of the University of Zurich. Two other Atlas records under this name lack a full given name or an affiliation, so only this paper is included.

highlights.STO2003: First author of the Drosophila Rheb paper.

Goberdhan DC.lab_name: Department of Physiology, Anatomy, and Genetics, University of Oxford (Oxford, UK)
Goberdhan DC.role: First author of a 2016 review on amino-acid sensing by mTORC1.
Goberdhan DC.sub: Department of Physiology, Anatomy, and Genetics, University of Oxford · Oxford, UK
story: This 2016 review argues that transporters inside the cell mark the spots where mTORC1 is switched on by amino acids. It covers late endosomes, lysosomes and the Golgi apparatus, and proposes that different amino acids in different compartments activate different mTORC1 complexes.
Deborah Goberdhan is first author. PubMed lists her at the Department of Physiology, Anatomy, and Genetics at the University of Oxford. This is a review, not new experiments.

Goul C.lab_name: Department of Molecular and Cell Biology, University of California, Berkeley (Berkeley, CA, USA)
Goul C.role: First author of a 2023 review on nutrient sensing by mTORC1.
Goul C.sub: Department of Molecular and Cell Biology, University of California, Berkeley · Berkeley, CA, USA
story: This 2023 review in Nature Reviews Molecular Cell Biology explains how mTORC1 reads nutrient signals, using recent structural and functional work on mTORC1 and its partners on the lysosome. It also covers how faulty nutrient signalling to mTORC1 contributes to diseases.
Claire Goul is first author. PubMed lists her at the Department of Molecular and Cell Biology, University of California, Berkeley. This is a review, not new experiments.

Gu X.lab_name: Whitehead Institute for Biomedical Research and Department of Biology, Massachusetts Institute of Technology (Cambridge, MA, USA)
Gu X.role: First author of the 2017 SAMTOR paper and middle author of three other nutrient-sensing papers from the same institute.
Gu X.sub: Whitehead Institute for Biomedical Research & Department of Biology, MIT · Cambridge, MA, USA
story: Xin Gu is first author of a 2017 cell study that found SAMTOR, a protein that senses S-adenosylmethionine (SAM), the cell's methyl donor. When methionine runs low, SAM falls, SAMTOR binds GATOR1 and mTORC1 signalling is reduced. This extends nutrient sensing from amino acids to a metabolite.

PubMed also lists Gu, at the same Whitehead Institute and MIT address, as a middle author of three further papers: the 2017 KICSTOR study (a complex that holds GATOR1 on the lysosome), the 2019 cryo-EM structure of Raptor docked on Rag-Ragulator, and the 2022 cryo-EM structure of GATOR2.

highlights.GU2017: First author of the SAMTOR paper.
highlights.WOL2017: Middle author of the KICSTOR paper.
highlights.ROG2019: Middle author of the cryo-EM paper on mTORC1 docking at the lysosome.
highlights.VAL2022: Middle author of the GATOR2 structure paper.

Guerrero-Morín JG.lab_name: Unidad Monterrey, Centro de Investigación y de Estudios Avanzados del IPN (Apodaca, Nuevo León, Mexico)
Guerrero-Morín JG.role: First author of a 2020 mathematical model of crosstalk between the circadian clock and mTORC1.
Guerrero-Morín JG.sub: Unidad Monterrey, Centro de Investigación y de Estudios Avanzados del IPN · Apodaca, Nuevo León, Mexico
story: This 2020 paper is a computer model, not an experiment. It asks how mTORC1 could change the body clock. The model suggests mTORC1 raises the size of clock oscillations by controlling translation of the clock protein BMAL1, and changes their period by controlling where BMAL1 sits in the cell.
José Guerrero-Morín is first author. PubMed lists him at the Monterrey unit of Cinvestav in Mexico.

highlights.GUE2020: First author of the modelling paper.

Guerra P.lab_name: Molecular Systems Biology, Groningen Biomolecular Sciences & Biotechnology Institute, University of Groningen (Groningen, The Netherlands)
Guerra P.role: First author of a 2022 yeast study on TORC1 and PKA activity across the cell cycle.
Guerra P.sub: Molecular Systems Biology, Groningen Biomolecular Sciences & Biotechnology Institute, University of Groningen · Groningen, The Netherlands
story: Using time-lapse microscopy on hundreds of budding yeast cells, this study found that TORC1 and PKA activity towards ribosome building rises and falls in step with the cell cycle, even when the surroundings stay constant. Mutations in upstream regulators suggest that internal metabolic signals drive part of this rhythm.
Paolo Guerra is first author. PubMed lists him in Molecular Systems Biology at the University of Groningen.

highlights.GUE2022: First author of the yeast cell-cycle study.

Heim MH.lab_name: Department of Biomedicine, University Hospital Basel (Basel, Switzerland)
Heim MH.role: Co-author of a 2017 mouse study showing that mTORC2 promotes liver cancer through lipid synthesis.
Heim MH.sub: Department of Biomedicine, University Hospital Basel · Basel, Switzerland
story: This 2017 study used a mouse model in which mTOR drives fatty liver that progresses to liver cancer. The team found that mTORC2 promotes de novo synthesis of fats and lipids, and that blocking fatty acid or sphingolipid synthesis prevented tumours. Higher lipid synthesis also tracked with mTORC2 activity in liver cancer patients.
Markus Heim is a middle author on the paper, and PubMed lists the affiliation shown here. Other Atlas records under this name show no affiliation in PubMed, so they are not included.

highlights.GUR2017: Middle author of the mTORC2 and lipid synthesis paper.

Jenoe P.role: Co-author of a 2017 mouse study showing that mTORC2 promotes liver cancer through lipid synthesis.
Jenoe P.sub: Biozentrum, University of Basel · Basel, Switzerland
story: This 2017 study used a mouse model in which mTOR drives fatty liver that progresses to liver cancer. The team found that mTORC2 promotes de novo synthesis of fats and lipids, and that blocking fatty acid or sphingolipid synthesis prevented tumours. Higher lipid synthesis also tracked with mTORC2 activity in liver cancer patients.
Paul Jenoe is a middle author on the paper, and PubMed lists the affiliation shown here. Other Atlas records under this name show no affiliation in PubMed, so they are not included.

highlights.GUR2017: Middle author of the mTORC2 and lipid synthesis paper.

Moes S.role: Co-author of a 2017 mouse study showing that mTORC2 promotes liver cancer through lipid synthesis.
Moes S.sub: Biozentrum, University of Basel · Basel, Switzerland
story: This 2017 study used a mouse model in which mTOR drives fatty liver that progresses to liver cancer. The team found that mTORC2 promotes de novo synthesis of fats and lipids, and that blocking fatty acid or sphingolipid synthesis prevented tumours. Higher lipid synthesis also tracked with mTORC2 activity in liver cancer patients.
Suzette Moes is a middle author on the paper, and PubMed lists the affiliation shown here. Other Atlas records under this name show no affiliation in PubMed, so they are not included.

highlights.GUR2017: Middle author of the mTORC2 and lipid synthesis paper.

Ahmed AAE.lab_name: Pharmacology and Toxicology Department, Faculty of Pharmacy, Helwan University (Ein Helwan, Egypt)
Ahmed AAE.role: Last author of a 2026 mouse study of melittin in psoriasis-like skin inflammation.
Ahmed AAE.sub: Pharmacology and Toxicology Department, Faculty of Pharmacy, Helwan University · Ein Helwan, Egypt
story: This 2026 mouse study tested melittin, the main component of bee venom, in imiquimod-induced psoriasis-like dermatitis. At the higher dose, melittin cut the clinical severity score by 60%. It also lowered PI3K/Akt/mTOR signalling and raised markers of autophagy. This is an animal study.
Amany Ahmed is the last author. PubMed lists her in the Pharmacology and Toxicology Department of the Faculty of Pharmacy at Helwan University.

highlights.HAFEZ2026: Last author of the melittin psoriasis study.

Hafez SA.lab_name: Health Holding Company, Aseer Health Cluster, Saudi Ministry of Health (Abha, Saudi Arabia)
Hafez SA.role: First author of a 2026 mouse study of melittin in psoriasis-like skin inflammation.
Hafez SA.sub: Health Holding Company, Aseer Health Cluster, Saudi Ministry of Health · Abha, Saudi Arabia
story: This 2026 mouse study tested melittin, the main component of bee venom, in imiquimod-induced psoriasis-like dermatitis. At the higher dose, melittin cut the clinical severity score by 60%. It also lowered PI3K/Akt/mTOR signalling and raised markers of autophagy. This is an animal study.
Saeed Hafez is first author. PubMed lists him at the Health Holding Company, Aseer Health Cluster, Saudi Ministry of Health in Abha.

highlights.HAFEZ2026: First author of the melittin psoriasis study.

Hagiwara A.role: First author of a 2012 mouse study on liver mTORC2 and glucose and fat metabolism.
Hagiwara A.sub: Biozentrum, University of Basel · Basel, Switzerland
story: The team deleted rictor, a core part of mTORC2, only in mouse liver. The liver then lost Akt Ser473 phosphorylation and kept making glucose while glycolysis and fat synthesis fell, as if it could not tell the animal had eaten. The mice developed high blood sugar and insulin and low blood lipids.
Asami Hagiwara is first author. PubMed lists her at the Biozentrum, University of Basel.

highlights.HAG2012: First author of the liver-specific rictor knockout study.

Polak P.role: First author of a 2008 mouse study on adipose-specific loss of raptor.
Polak P.sub: Biozentrum, University of Basel · Basel, Switzerland
story: Mice lacking raptor, an essential part of mTORC1, only in fat tissue were lean, protected from diet-induced obesity and more insulin sensitive. Their fat showed higher energy use through mitochondrial uncoupling. This shows a role for mTORC1 in fat metabolism, in mice.
Pazit Polak is first author. PubMed lists her at the Biozentrum, University of Basel. A second Atlas record under this name shows no affiliation, so it is not included.

highlights.POL2008: First author of the adipose raptor knockout paper.

Han JM.lab_name: Medicinal Bioconvergence Research Center, Seoul National University (Seoul, Republic of Korea)
Han JM.role: First author of a 2012 cell study identifying leucyl-tRNA synthetase as a leucine sensor for mTORC1.
Han JM.sub: Medicinal Bioconvergence Research Center, Seoul National University · Seoul, Republic of Korea
story: This 2012 study found that leucyl-tRNA synthetase (LRS), an enzyme that attaches leucine to its tRNA, also senses the leucine level inside cells. LRS binds the Rag GTPase and acts as its GAP in an amino-acid-dependent way, which activates mTORC1. The work was done in cells.
Jung Min Han is first author. PubMed lists him at the Medicinal Bioconvergence Research Center at Seoul National University.

highlights.HAN2012: First author of the LRS leucine sensor paper.

Hands JM.lab_name: The George Washington University School of Medicine and Health Sciences (Washington, DC, USA)
Hands JM.role: First author of a 2025 review of clinical evidence for off-label rapamycin in healthy adults.
Hands JM.sub: The George Washington University School of Medicine and Health Sciences · Washington, DC, USA
story: This 2025 review looks at human evidence for low-dose rapamycin and related drugs in healthy adults, and re-models one cohort with the PhenoAge biological-age clock. Its conclusion is cautious: animal lifespan data are strong, but human data have not yet shown that rapamycin delays aging in healthy people.
Jacob Hands is first author. PubMed lists him at The George Washington University School of Medicine and Health Sciences.

Rosen B.role: Last author of a 2025 review of clinical evidence for off-label rapamycin in healthy adults.
Rosen B.sub: mTOR Medicine Practitioner · Los Angeles, CA, USA
story: This 2025 review looks at human evidence for low-dose rapamycin and related drugs in healthy adults, and re-models one cohort with the PhenoAge biological-age clock. Its conclusion is cautious: animal lifespan data are strong, but human data have not yet shown that rapamycin delays aging in healthy people.
Bradley Rosen is the last author. PubMed lists his affiliation only as mTOR Medicine Practitioner, Los Angeles.

Javors MA.lab_name: Department of Psychiatry, University of Texas Health Science Center at San Antonio (San Antonio, TX, USA)
Javors MA.role: Middle author of a 2018 pilot trial of rapamycin in older adults and a 2022 mouse lifespan study.
Javors MA.sub: Barshop Institute & Department of Psychiatry, University of Texas Health Science Center at San Antonio · San Antonio, TX, USA
story: Martin Javors is a middle author of a 2018 randomised pilot trial in 25 healthy adults aged 70 to 95. Daily rapamycin for at least 8 weeks was tolerated, with small red-blood-cell changes and no rise in blood glucose or insulin resistance in that short window.

He is also a middle author of a 2022 NIA Interventions Testing Program paper in mice. Rapamycin plus acarbose started at 9 months gave male mice a longer lifespan than rapamycin alone in earlier cohorts, while females did about the same as on rapamycin alone. PubMed lists him at the University of Texas Health Science Center at San Antonio in both papers. Five more Atlas records under this name carry no affiliation and are not included.

highlights.KRA2018: Middle author of the older-adult rapamycin pilot trial.
highlights.STR2022: Middle author of the ITP rapamycin plus acarbose and captopril paper.

Fernandez E.lab_name: Barshop Institute for Longevity and Aging Studies, University of Texas Health Science Center at San Antonio (San Antonio, TX, USA)
Fernandez E.role: Middle author of two marmoset rapamycin studies and a 2022 mouse lifespan study.
Fernandez E.sub: Barshop Institute for Longevity and Aging Studies, University of Texas Health Science Center at San Antonio · San Antonio, TX, USA
story: Elizabeth Fernandez is a middle author of two studies of oral rapamycin in the common marmoset, a small monkey. The 2014 study set out dosing and blood levels and saw reduced mTORC1 signalling in treated animals. The 2015 study found only minor metabolic effects of long-term treatment.

She is also a middle author of a 2022 NIA Interventions Testing Program paper in mice, where rapamycin plus acarbose gave males a longer lifespan than rapamycin alone in earlier cohorts. PubMed lists her at the Barshop Institute, University of Texas Health Science Center at San Antonio, in all three. Five more Atlas records under this name carry no affiliation and are not included.

highlights.TAR2014: Middle author of the marmoset rapamycin dosing study.
highlights.ROS2015: Middle author of the marmoset metabolic study.
highlights.STR2022: Middle author of the ITP rapamycin plus acarbose and captopril paper.

Nelson JF.lab_name: Department of Cellular and Integrative Physiology, Barshop Institute for Longevity and Aging Studies, University of Texas Health Science Center at San Antonio (San Antonio, TX, USA)
Nelson JF.role: Middle author of a 2022 NIA Interventions Testing Program mouse lifespan study.
Nelson JF.sub: Barshop Institute for Longevity and Aging Studies, University of Texas Health Science Center at San Antonio · San Antonio, TX, USA
story: This 2022 mouse study from the NIA Interventions Testing Program found that rapamycin plus acarbose started at 9 months gave male mice a longer lifespan than rapamycin alone in earlier cohorts. In females the combination did about the same as rapamycin alone. Captopril gave a small lifespan gain in females.

James Nelson is a middle author. PubMed lists him in the Department of Cellular and Integrative Physiology, Barshop Institute, University of Texas Health Science Center at San Antonio. Five other Atlas records under this name carry no affiliation and are not included.

highlights.STR2022: Middle author of the ITP combination study.

Wilkinson JE.lab_name: Unit for Laboratory Animal Medicine and Department of Pathology, University of Michigan (Ann Arbor, MI, USA)
Wilkinson JE.role: First author of a 2012 mouse study showing that rapamycin slows several aspects of aging.
Wilkinson JE.sub: Unit for Laboratory Animal Medicine & Department of Pathology, University of Michigan · Ann Arbor, MI, USA
story: This 2012 mouse study asked whether rapamycin only prevents the cancers that kill mice, or slows aging more widely. Age-related changes in heart, liver, adrenal glands, endometrium and tendon, and the decline in spontaneous activity, all came on more slowly in treated mice. The mice also had more testicular degeneration and cataracts.

John Wilkinson is first author. PubMed lists him at the Unit for Laboratory Animal Medicine and Department of Pathology, University of Michigan. Three other Atlas records use the name form J Erby Wilkinson without an affiliation, so they are not included.

highlights.WIL2012: First author of the rapamycin and aging paper.

Allison DB.lab_name: Department of Biostatistics, University of Alabama (Birmingham, AL, USA)
Allison DB.role: Middle author of a 2017 comparison of two caloric restriction studies in rhesus monkeys.
Allison DB.sub: Department of Biostatistics, University of Alabama · Birmingham, AL, USA
story: This 2017 paper compared the long-term caloric restriction studies on rhesus monkeys run by the National Institute on Aging and by the University of Wisconsin. It supports health benefits from caloric restriction in both, while the effect on survival depended on study design and on what the control monkeys ate.

David Allison is a middle author, and PubMed lists him in the Department of Biostatistics at the University of Alabama, Birmingham. A second Atlas record under this name carries no affiliation, so it is not included.

highlights.MAT2017: Middle author of the monkey caloric restriction comparison.

He Y.lab_name: Department of Endocrinology, Tongji Hospital, Tongji Medical College, Huazhong University of Science and Technology (Wuhan, Hubei, China)
He Y.role: First author of a 2026 study in mice and a human cohort linking the blood hormone ANGPTL8 to fat-tissue ageing through the AKT-mTOR pathway.
He Y.sub: Department of Endocrinology, Tongji Hospital, Tongji Medical College, Huazhong University of Science & Technology, Wuhan, China
story: Yi He is first author of an Atlas study (HE2026) on ANGPTL8, a hormone made in fat tissue. In a large group of people, higher blood ANGPTL8 went with older biological age and higher risk of death. In mice, deleting the Angptl8 gene lengthened life and lowered ageing markers in fat. In cells, ANGPTL8 bound AKT2 and switched on the AKT-mTOR-S6K pathway, which pushed fat cells into senescence. PubMed lists He at the Department of Endocrinology, Tongji Hospital, in Wuhan.

highlights.HE2026: First author: led the report that ANGPTL8 drives fat-cell senescence through AKT2 and mTOR, with human cohort data and Angptl8-knockout mice.

Hennessy-Strahs S.lab_name: Immunobiology and Transplant Science Center and Department of Surgery, Houston Methodist Hospital (Houston, Texas, USA)
Hennessy-Strahs S.role: First author of a 2026 mouse and cell-culture study showing that alveolar macrophages need mTOR to survive.
Hennessy-Strahs S.sub: Naresh K. Vashisht College of Medicine, Texas A&M University (Bryan, Texas) · Immunobiology and Transplant Science Center, Houston Methodist Hospital (Houston, Texas)
story: Samson Hennessy-Strahs is first author of an Atlas study (HEN2026) on the immune cells that clear surfactant from the lungs, called alveolar macrophages. In mice, removing mTOR from myeloid cells, or treating the animals with the mTOR inhibitor temsirolimus, steadily wiped out these macrophages and caused a lung condition resembling pulmonary alveolar proteinosis. The work points to a possible cause of lung side effects seen with mTOR-inhibitor drugs. PubMed lists him at Texas A&M University and at Houston Methodist Hospital.

highlights.HEN2026: First author: reported that deleting or drugging mTOR in mice depletes alveolar macrophages and produces lung disease like that seen with mTOR-inhibitor drugs.

Holz MK.lab_name: Department of Cell Biology, Harvard Medical School (Boston, Massachusetts, USA)
Holz MK.role: First author of a 2005 cell study on how mTOR and S6K1 assemble the translation preinitiation complex on eIF3.
Holz MK.sub: Department of Cell Biology, Harvard Medical School, Boston, Massachusetts
story: Marina K. Holz is first author of an Atlas study (HOL2005) in human cell lines about how cells start making proteins. The paper showed that mTOR and the enzyme S6K1 move on and off a protein platform called eIF3 in a set order. When S6K1 is idle it sits on eIF3. After cell stimulation, mTOR with raptor arrives, phosphorylates S6K1, and S6K1 leaves to act on its targets. PubMed lists her at the Department of Cell Biology, Harvard Medical School.

highlights.HOL2005: First author: showed in cultured cells that mTOR/raptor and S6K1 swap places on the eIF3 complex as part of switching on translation.

Horvath S.lab_name: Department of Human Genetics, David Geffen School of Medicine, University of California, Los Angeles (Los Angeles, California, USA)
Horvath S.role: First author of a 2021 study building DNA methylation clocks for common marmosets and testing whether rapamycin changes epigenetic age.
Horvath S.sub: Department of Human Genetics, David Geffen School of Medicine, University of California, Los Angeles
story: Steve Horvath is first author of an Atlas study (HOR2021) in common marmosets, a small primate. The team built two epigenetic clocks, which estimate age from DNA methylation in blood. The clock that works across species also tracked age in vervet monkeys and rhesus macaques. In a separate group of marmosets given rapamycin, the clocks did not detect a significant change in epigenetic age. PubMed lists him at UCLA, in the Department of Human Genetics.

highlights.HOR2021: First author: reported marmoset epigenetic clocks and found that they showed no significant effect of rapamycin on blood epigenetic age.

Mattison JA.role: First author of a 2017 comparison of two rhesus monkey caloric restriction studies and co-author of a 2021 marmoset rapamycin epigenetic clock study.
Mattison JA.sub: Translational Gerontology Branch, National Institute on Aging, National Institutes of Health (PubMed lists Baltimore and Dickerson, Maryland)
story: Julie A. Mattison is first author of an Atlas study (MAT2017) that compared two long-running caloric restriction studies in rhesus monkeys, one at the National Institute on Aging and one at the University of Wisconsin. Putting the data side by side, the authors found health benefits from eating less in both, and saw that survival results depended on study design and on what the control animals ate.

She is also a co-author of the 2021 marmoset paper (HOR2021), which built epigenetic age clocks and found no significant effect of rapamycin on them. In both papers PubMed lists her at the Translational Gerontology Branch of the National Institute on Aging.

highlights.MAT2017: First author: led the direct comparison of the NIA and Wisconsin rhesus monkey caloric restriction studies.
highlights.HOR2021: Co-author: listed in the NIA Translational Gerontology Branch on the marmoset epigenetic clock and rapamycin study.

Hosokawa N.lab_name: Department of Physiology and Cell Biology, Tokyo Medical and Dental University (Tokyo, Japan)
Hosokawa N.role: First author of a 2009 cell study showing that nutrient-dependent mTORC1 binding to the ULK1-Atg13-FIP200 complex is needed for autophagy control.
Hosokawa N.sub: Department of Physiology and Cell Biology, Tokyo Medical and Dental University, Tokyo
story: Nao Hosokawa is first author of an Atlas study (HOS2009) in cultured cells on how mTORC1 holds back autophagy, the cell's recycling process. The group found that Atg13 forms a large complex with ULK1 and FIP200, and that mTORC1 joins this complex when nutrients are plentiful and phosphorylates ULK1 and Atg13. Starvation or rapamycin releases that brake and autophagy can begin. PubMed lists Hosokawa at Tokyo Medical and Dental University.

highlights.HOS2009: First author: reported that mTORC1 joins and phosphorylates the ULK1-Atg13-FIP200 complex in a nutrient-dependent way to suppress autophagy.

Talbott G.lab_name: Department of Genetics and Complex Diseases, Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health (Boston, Massachusetts, USA)
Talbott G.role: Co-author of two mTORC1 studies from the Manning lab setting, one on metformin in mouse liver and one on the TSC complex at the lysosome.
Talbott G.sub: Department of Genetics and Complex Diseases, Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health, Boston, Massachusetts
story: George Talbott is a co-author of two Atlas studies, both listing him at the Department of Genetics and Complex Diseases at Harvard. In HOW2017, work in mouse liver and liver cells showed that metformin switches off mTORC1, and that at the lowest doses this needs AMPK and the TSC complex. In MEN2014, cell experiments showed that insulin makes the TSC complex leave the lysosome surface, which lets mTORC1 turn on.
He is a middle author on both papers. PubMed shows no more about his role than his place in the author list.

highlights.HOW2017: Middle author on the paper showing metformin inhibits mTORC1 in mouse liver through AMPK and the TSC complex.
highlights.MEN2014: Middle author on the paper showing the TSC complex moves off the lysosome in response to insulin.

Turner M.lab_name: Department of Genetics and Complex Diseases, Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health (Boston, Massachusetts, USA)
Turner M.role: Co-author of two mTORC1 studies from the Manning lab setting, one on nucleotide synthesis in TSC-deficient cells and one on metformin in mouse liver.
Turner M.sub: Department of Genetics and Complex Diseases, Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health, Boston, Massachusetts
story: Marc Turner is a co-author of two Atlas studies, both listing him at the Department of Genetics and Complex Diseases at Harvard. VAL2017 found that cells with overactive mTORC1 make so much ribosomal RNA that their nucleotide supply runs short, which makes them sensitive to drugs that block guanine nucleotide synthesis, shown in cells and mouse tumor models. HOW2017 showed that metformin inhibits mTORC1 in mouse liver through AMPK and the TSC complex.
He is a middle author on both papers. PubMed shows no more about his role than his place in the author list.

highlights.VAL2017: Middle author on the paper linking mTORC1 activity to nucleotide demand and a drug-sensitive weakness in TSC-deficient cells.
highlights.HOW2017: Middle author on the paper showing metformin inhibits mTORC1 in mouse liver through AMPK and the TSC complex.

Huang W.lab_name: Department of Neuroscience, Baylor College of Medicine (Houston, Texas, USA)
Huang W.role: First author of a 2013 mouse and fly study showing mTORC2 is needed for actin changes that support long-term memory.
Huang W.sub: Department of Neuroscience, Baylor College of Medicine, Houston, Texas
story: Wei Huang is first author of an Atlas study (HUA2013) on memory. Mice lacking Rictor, a key part of mTORC2, in the forebrain had weaker long-term memory and weaker late-phase long-term potentiation, a lasting strengthening of connections between neurons. Flies lacking dTORC2 also had a long-term memory problem. Hippocampal actin polymerization was low in the mice, and restoring it fixed both defects. PubMed lists Huang at the Department of Neuroscience, Baylor College of Medicine.

highlights.HUA2013: First author: showed that deleting Rictor in mouse forebrain lowers mTORC2 activity, actin polymerization and long-term memory.

Huang C.lab_name: Department of Radiation Oncology, The Affiliated Hospital of Inner Mongolia Medical University (Hohhot, China)
Huang C.role: First author of a 2026 study in cervical cancer samples, cells and mice on how the PIK3CA E545K mutation drives AKT/mTOR signalling.
Huang C.sub: Department of Radiation Oncology, The Affiliated Hospital of Inner Mongolia Medical University, Hohhot, China
story: Congxiu Huang is first author of an Atlas study (HUANG2026) on cervical cancer. The team sequenced tumors from 61 patients and found PIK3CA among the most often mutated genes. In cancer cell lines, the E545K mutation made cells grow and invade more and die less, with stronger AKT/mTOR signalling. A mouse xenograft experiment, where human cells are grown as tumors in mice, agreed with this. PubMed lists Huang at the Department of Radiation Oncology, Affiliated Hospital of Inner Mongolia Medical University.

highlights.HUANG2026: First author: reported that the PIK3CA E545K mutation boosts cervical cancer cell growth and invasion through AKT/mTOR signalling.

Hudes G.lab_name: Department of Medical Oncology, Fox Chase Cancer Center (Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, USA)
Hudes G.role: First author of the 2007 phase 3 trial comparing temsirolimus, interferon alfa, or both in advanced kidney cancer.
Hudes G.sub: Department of Medical Oncology, Fox Chase Cancer Center, Philadelphia, Pennsylvania
story: Gary Hudes is first author of an Atlas study (HUD2007), a phase 3 randomized trial in people with poor-prognosis metastatic kidney cancer. Among 626 patients, those given temsirolimus, an mTOR inhibitor, lived a median of 10.9 months, compared with 7.3 months on interferon alfa. Adding temsirolimus to interferon did not help. Rash, high blood sugar and high blood lipids were more common with temsirolimus. PubMed lists Hudes at the Fox Chase Cancer Center.

highlights.HUD2007: First author: reported the phase 3 trial in which temsirolimus alone gave longer survival than interferon alfa in poor-prognosis kidney cancer.

Yang Q.lab_name: Life Sciences Institute, University of Michigan (Ann Arbor, Michigan, USA)
Yang Q.role: First author of a 2006 cell and mouse study identifying Sin1 as an essential component of the TORC2 complex.
Yang Q.sub: Life Sciences Institute, University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, Michigan
story: Qian Yang is first author of an Atlas study (YAN2006) on mTOR complex 2. Using fly and human cells and mouse genetics, the paper showed that Sin1 is part of TORC2 but not TORC1. Lowering Sin1 reduced Akt phosphorylation and broke the link between Rictor and mTOR, and TORC2 needed Sin1 to be active in a test tube. PubMed lists Yang at the Life Sciences Institute, University of Michigan. The same name also appears as a middle author on two other Atlas papers, but PubMed gives no affiliation there, so those were not counted.

highlights.YAN2006: First author: showed that Sin1 is an essential TORC2 component needed for complex formation and for Akt phosphorylation.

Iyer G.lab_name: Human Oncology and Pathogenesis Program, Memorial Sloan-Kettering Cancer Center (New York, New York, USA)
Iyer G.role: First author of a 2012 genome sequencing study linking TSC1 mutation to a strong response to everolimus in bladder cancer.
Iyer G.sub: Human Oncology and Pathogenesis Program, Memorial Sloan-Kettering Cancer Center, New York
story: Gopa Iyer is first author of an Atlas study (IYE2012) that began with one bladder cancer patient who had a long remission on the mTOR inhibitor everolimus. Whole-genome sequencing of that tumor found a loss-of-function mutation in TSC1, a brake on mTOR. Checking 109 more bladder cancers, about 8 percent had TSC1 mutations, and these tracked with everolimus sensitivity. The starting point was a single patient, so it raises a hypothesis more than it proves one. PubMed lists Iyer at Memorial Sloan-Kettering Cancer Center.

highlights.IYE2012: First author: reported the genome sequencing of an exceptional everolimus responder and the link to TSC1 loss in bladder cancer.

Jackson LN.lab_name: Department of Biomedical Sciences, University of South Alabama (Mobile, Alabama, USA)
Jackson LN.role: First author of a 2026 fruit fly study showing that rapamycin can lengthen or shorten life depending on the diet.
Jackson LN.sub: Department of Biomedical Sciences, University of South Alabama, Mobile, Alabama
story: Lauren N. Jackson is first author of an Atlas study (JAC2026) in Drosophila fruit flies. Across five fly strains, rapamycin was harmful in 19 of 26 experiments on a cornmeal and torula yeast food. On a richer brewer's yeast food it helped in 8 experiments, did nothing in 14, and was never clearly harmful. Effects on median lifespan ranged from a 51 percent loss to a 5 percent gain, and depended on sex and strain. PubMed lists Jackson at the University of South Alabama.

highlights.JAC2026: First author: reported that rapamycin's effect on fly lifespan flips between harmful and helpful depending on diet, sex and strain.

Kim YC.lab_name: Department of Pharmacology and Moores Cancer Center, University of California, San Diego (La Jolla, California, USA)
Kim YC.role: Co-author of a 2015 cell study showing that glutamine activates mTORC1 by a route different from leucine.
Kim YC.sub: Department of Pharmacology and Moores Cancer Center, University of California, San Diego, La Jolla, California
story: Young Chul Kim is a co-author of an Atlas study (JEW2015) on how amino acids switch on mTORC1. In cultured cells, leucine acted through the Rag GTPases, while glutamine could activate mTORC1 without them, through a route that needed the small GTPase Arf1. PubMed lists Kim as the second author, at the Department of Pharmacology and Moores Cancer Center, UC San Diego. The name also appears on a second Atlas paper (PAR2014), but PubMed gives no affiliations there, so that one was not counted.

highlights.JEW2015: Second author on the paper showing glutamine activates mTORC1 independently of the Rag GTPases.

Park HW.lab_name: Department of Pharmacology and Moores Cancer Center, University of California, San Diego (La Jolla, California, USA)
Park HW.role: Co-author of a 2015 cell study showing that glutamine activates mTORC1 by a route different from leucine.
Park HW.sub: Department of Pharmacology and Moores Cancer Center, University of California, San Diego, La Jolla, California
story: Hyun Woo Park is a co-author of an Atlas study (JEW2015) on how amino acids switch on mTORC1. In cultured cells, leucine acted through the Rag GTPases, while glutamine could activate mTORC1 without them, through a route that needed the small GTPase Arf1. PubMed lists Park, in the fifth author position, at the Department of Pharmacology and Moores Cancer Center, UC San Diego. The name also appears on a second Atlas paper (RUS2013), but PubMed gives no affiliation for him there, so that one was not counted.

highlights.JEW2015: Fifth author on the paper showing glutamine activates mTORC1 independently of the Rag GTPases.

Jung J.lab_name: Institute of Biochemistry II, Goethe University School of Medicine (Frankfurt am Main, Germany)
Jung J.role: First author of a 2015 cell study identifying the lysosomal protein SLC38A9 as a member of the Rag-Ragulator complex that passes amino acid signals to mTORC1.
Jung J.sub: Institute of Biochemistry II, Goethe University School of Medicine, Frankfurt am Main, Germany
story: Jennifer Jung is first author of an Atlas study (JUN2015) in human cells. The paper found that SLC38A9, a protein in the lysosome membrane, sits with the Rag GTPases and the Ragulator complex. Removing SLC38A9 lowered mTORC1 activity when amino acids were present, and too much SLC38A9 made mTORC1 overactive. PubMed lists Jung at the Institute of Biochemistry II, Goethe University Frankfurt.

highlights.JUN2015: First author: reported SLC38A9 as a Rag-Ragulator component that relays amino acid availability to mTORC1.

Jin P.lab_name: College of Pharmaceutical Sciences, Southwest University (Chongqing, China)
Jin P.role: First author of a 2026 cell study showing that oxidative stress drives P-glycoprotein production through an mTOR-eIF4A pathway.
Jin P.sub: College of Pharmaceutical Sciences, Southwest University, Chongqing, China
story: Peng Jin is first author of an Atlas study (JIN2026) on drug resistance in cells. The paper reports that oxidative stress switches on a PI3K-AKT-mTORC1-eIF4A chain that quickly raises production of P-glycoprotein, a pump that expels drugs. This works by changing translation of the mRNA rather than by turning up the gene. PubMed lists Jin at the College of Pharmaceutical Sciences, Southwest University.

highlights.JIN2026: First author: reported the redox-sensitive mTOR-eIF4A route that boosts P-glycoprotein translation.

Jin L.lab_name: Department of Cardiology, The Second Affiliated Hospital of Xi'an Jiaotong University (Xi'an, Shaanxi, China)
Jin L.role: First author of a 2026 mouse study on rapamycin and age-related atrial fibrillation.
Jin L.sub: Department of Cardiology, The Second Affiliated Hospital of Xi'an Jiaotong University, Xi'an, China
story: Lingyan Jin is first author of an Atlas study (JIN2026B) in mice aged with D-galactose injections. Rapamycin in the diet lowered the animals' susceptibility to atrial fibrillation and eased changes in the structure and electrical behavior of the heart's upper chambers. The effect ran mainly through lower HIF-1 alpha activity and did not depend on mTOR, which is an unusual result for a rapamycin study. PubMed lists Jin at the Department of Cardiology, Second Affiliated Hospital of Xi'an Jiaotong University.

highlights.JIN2026B: First author: reported that rapamycin reduced atrial fibrillation susceptibility in aged mice through HIF-1 alpha, independent of mTOR.

Zheng Q.lab_name: Department of Cardiology, The Second Affiliated Hospital of Xi'an Jiaotong University (Xi'an, Shaanxi, China)
Zheng Q.role: Senior (last) author of a 2026 mouse study on rapamycin and age-related atrial fibrillation.
Zheng Q.sub: Department of Cardiology, The Second Affiliated Hospital of Xi'an Jiaotong University, Xi'an, China
story: Qiangsun Zheng is last author of an Atlas study (JIN2026B) in mice aged with D-galactose injections. Rapamycin in the diet lowered the animals' susceptibility to atrial fibrillation and eased changes in the structure of the heart's upper chambers. The effect ran mainly through lower HIF-1 alpha activity and did not depend on mTOR. PubMed lists Zheng at the Department of Cardiology, Second Affiliated Hospital of Xi'an Jiaotong University, and as a corresponding author.

highlights.JIN2026B: Last author: senior author of the study showing rapamycin reduces atrial fibrillation in aged mice through HIF-1 alpha, independent of mTOR.

de Mol J.lab_name: Division of BioTherapeutics, Leiden Academic Centre for Drug Research, Leiden University (Leiden, the Netherlands)
de Mol J.role: First author of a 2026 mouse study on how rapamycin reshapes immune responses in aged atherosclerotic plaques.
de Mol J.sub: Division of BioTherapeutics, Leiden Academic Centre for Drug Research, Leiden University, the Netherlands
story: Jill de Mol is first author of an Atlas study (JIN2026C) in old mice with atherosclerosis. Rapamycin treatment for 8 weeks lowered the number of macrophages in plaques and cut total T cell numbers. It moved CD8 T cells from an effector to a central-memory type, raised regulatory T cells, and reduced germinal-center B cells and antibody levels. PubMed lists de Mol at the Leiden Academic Centre for Drug Research, Leiden University.

highlights.JIN2026C: First author: reported that rapamycin shifts the immune cell mix in aged atherosclerotic mice toward regulatory and away from inflammatory responses.

Johnson SC.lab_name: Department of Pathology, University of Washington (Seattle, Washington, USA)
Johnson SC.role: First author of a 2013 review in Nature on mTOR as a regulator of ageing and age-related disease.
Johnson SC.sub: Department of Pathology, University of Washington, Seattle, Washington
story: Simon C. Johnson is first author of an Atlas review (JOH2013), meaning it summarizes earlier work and has no new experiments. It argues that blocking the mTOR pathway lengthens life in several species and protects against a growing list of age-related diseases. It also notes that side effects of current mTOR inhibitors make them unsuitable for healthy people. PubMed lists Johnson at the Department of Pathology, University of Washington.

highlights.JOH2013: First author: wrote the Nature review that summarizes mTOR's role in ageing and age-related disease.

Powers RW.lab_name: Department of Genome Sciences and Medicine, University of Washington (Seattle, Washington, USA)
Powers RW.role: First author of a 2006 yeast study showing that lower TOR signalling extends chronological lifespan.
Powers RW.sub: Department of Genome Sciences and Medicine, University of Washington, Seattle, Washington
story: R Wilson Powers is first author of an Atlas study (POW2006) in baker's yeast. The team screened about 4,800 gene-deletion strains for survival of non-dividing cells and found long-lived strains with mutations in the TOR pathway. Rapamycin and removing some amino acids from the medium also extended survival, and the longer-lived cells were more stress resistant. PubMed lists Powers at the University of Washington, Seattle. His name also appears on a second Atlas yeast paper (KAE2005), but PubMed gives no affiliation for him there, so it was not counted.

highlights.POW2006: First author: reported that lowering TOR signalling extends chronological lifespan in yeast.

Kalender A.lab_name: Department of Cancer and Cell Biology, Metabolic Diseases Institute, University of Cincinnati (Cincinnati, Ohio, USA)
Kalender A.role: First author of a 2010 cell and mouse study showing that metformin inhibits mTORC1 without AMPK, through the Rag GTPases.
Kalender A.sub: Department of Cancer and Cell Biology, Metabolic Diseases Institute, University of Cincinnati, Ohio
story: Adem Kalender is first author of an Atlas study (KAL2010) on how metformin acts. In cells lacking AMPK or the TSC1/TSC2 proteins, metformin and phenformin still inhibited mTORC1, and the effect needed the Rag GTPases. Two mouse models, one for cancer and one for diabetes, agreed that metformin can suppress mTORC1 without AMPK. PubMed lists Kalender at the University of Cincinnati.

highlights.KAL2010: First author: reported that biguanides inhibit mTORC1 independently of AMPK and TSC, through the Rag GTPases.

Pacold ME.lab_name: Department of Biology, Massachusetts Institute of Technology (Cambridge, Massachusetts, USA)
Pacold ME.role: Co-author of a 2015 structural study of how Sestrin2 binds leucine to signal to mTORC1.
Pacold ME.sub: Department of Biology, Massachusetts Institute of Technology, and Whitehead Institute, Cambridge, Massachusetts
story: Michael E. Pacold is a co-author of an Atlas study (SAX2015) that solved the crystal structure of Sestrin2 bound to leucine. The structure shows a single pocket that holds leucine, closed by a lid-like loop. A mutation that weakens leucine binding raised the amount of leucine cells needed to activate mTORC1. PubMed lists Pacold as the fourth author, at the Department of Biology, MIT, and the Whitehead Institute. His name also appears on a 2013 Atlas paper (KAN2013), but PubMed gives no affiliation for him there, so it was not counted.

highlights.SAX2015: Fourth author on the crystal structure of Sestrin2 with leucine, the structural basis of leucine sensing by mTORC1.

Zid BM.lab_name: California Institute of Technology (Pasadena, California, USA)
Zid BM.role: First author of a 2009 fruit fly study showing that 4E-BP is required for dietary restriction to extend lifespan.
Zid BM.sub: California Institute of Technology, Pasadena, California
story: Brian M. Zid is first author of an Atlas study (ZID2009) in Drosophila. On a restricted diet, flies made more of the protein 4E-BP, an mTOR target. This raised translation of nuclear-encoded mitochondrial genes, and 4E-BP was needed for the lifespan gain. PubMed lists Zid at the California Institute of Technology. His name also appears as a second author on a 2004 Atlas paper (KAP2004), but PubMed gives no affiliation for him there, so it was not counted.

highlights.ZID2009: First author: showed that 4E-BP boosts mitochondrial gene translation and is required for lifespan extension on dietary restriction in flies.

Karuppasamy M.lab_name: European Molecular Biology Laboratory, Grenoble Outstation (Grenoble, France)
Karuppasamy M.role: First author of a 2017 cryo-EM structure of yeast TORC2.
Karuppasamy M.sub: European Molecular Biology Laboratory, Grenoble Outstation, France
story: Manikandan Karuppasamy is first author of an Atlas study (KAR2017) that used electron cryo-microscopy to determine the structure of TORC2 from baker's yeast. The complex has six subunits. Its Avo3 (Rictor) part covers the site where the FKBP12-rapamycin drug complex would attach, which helps explain why TORC2 resists rapamycin. PubMed lists Karuppasamy at the EMBL Grenoble Outstation.

highlights.KAR2017: First author: reported the cryo-EM structure of yeast TORC2 and what it shows about rapamycin insensitivity.

Kelly G.lab_name: Biosciences Institute, Faculty of Medical Sciences, Newcastle University (Newcastle upon Tyne, UK)
Kelly G.role: First author of a 2024 study in human cells showing that basal mitophagy falls in senescence and can be restored.
Kelly G.sub: Biosciences Institute, Faculty of Medical Sciences, Newcastle University, UK
story: George Kelly is first author of an Atlas study (KEL2024) in primary human cells. Healthy cells ran a steady level of mitophagy, the removal of damaged mitochondria, through the PINK1/Parkin pathway with p62 as the receptor. This shut down as cells became senescent or old. Blocking mitophagy in young cells triggered senescence, and restarting it was needed for rapamycin and NAD precursors to work against senescence. PubMed lists Kelly at the Biosciences Institute, Newcastle University.

highlights.KEL2024: First author: reported that suppressed basal mitophagy drives senescence in human cells and that a p62-targeting small molecule can reverse it.

Khapre RV.lab_name: Center for Gene Regulation in Health and Diseases, Cleveland State University (Cleveland, Ohio, USA)
Khapre RV.role: First author of a 2014 mouse and cell study showing that the clock protein BMAL1 restrains mTORC1 and affects ageing.
Khapre RV.sub: Center for Gene Regulation in Health and Diseases, Cleveland State University, Ohio
story: Rohini V. Khapre is first author of an Atlas study (KHA2014) on the circadian clock and ageing. Mice and cells lacking the clock protein BMAL1 had higher mTORC1 activity. Treating Bmal1 knockout mice with rapamycin raised their lifespan by 50 percent, which suggests BMAL1 normally acts as a brake on mTORC1. PubMed lists Khapre at the Center for Gene Regulation in Health and Diseases, Cleveland State University.

highlights.KHA2014: First author: reported that BMAL1 deficiency raises mTORC1 activity and that rapamycin lengthens life in Bmal1 knockout mice.

Kidani Y.lab_name: Institute for Molecular Medicine, David Geffen School of Medicine, University of California, Los Angeles (Los Angeles, California, USA)
Kidani Y.role: First author of a 2013 mouse and cell study showing that SREBP proteins drive the metabolic programming of effector T cells.
Kidani Y.sub: Institute for Molecular Medicine, David Geffen School of Medicine, University of California, Los Angeles
story: Yoko Kidani is first author of an Atlas study (KID2013) on activated CD8 T cells. These cells quickly switch on fat and cholesterol synthesis, and the paper showed that this switch depends on SREBP proteins. Without SREBP signaling, T cells could not blast and expand well during a viral infection in mice. The Atlas notes that the switch runs through PI3K and mTOR, and that rapamycin blocked it in cells. PubMed lists Kidani at the Institute for Molecular Medicine, UCLA.

highlights.KID2013: First author: showed that SREBPs are needed for effector T cell growth and that the lipid programme runs through mTOR.

Kim YM.lab_name: Department of Biochemistry, University of Minnesota (Minneapolis, Minnesota, USA)
Kim YM.role: First author of a 2012 cell study identifying SH3BP4 as a negative regulator of amino acid signaling to mTORC1.
Kim YM.sub: Department of Biochemistry, University of Minnesota, Minneapolis, Minnesota
story: Young-Mi Kim is first author of an Atlas study (KIM2012) in human cells. The paper found that SH3BP4 binds the inactive Rag GTPase complex when amino acids are scarce and stops it from becoming active. This keeps mTORC1 away from the lysosome, lowers mTORC1 activity and cell growth, and favors autophagy. PubMed lists Kim at the Department of Biochemistry, University of Minnesota.

highlights.KIM2012: First author: reported SH3BP4 as a negative regulator of the Rag GTPase complex and amino acid-driven mTORC1 activation.

Benavides AD.lab_name: Department of Microbiology, Immunology, and Molecular Genetics, The University of Texas Health Science Center (San Antonio, Texas, USA)
Benavides AD.role: Co-author of a 2018 randomized pilot trial of rapamycin safety in healthy older adults.
Benavides AD.sub: Department of Microbiology, Immunology, and Molecular Genetics, The University of Texas Health Science Center, San Antonio
story: Adriana D. Benavides is a co-author of an Atlas study (KRA2018), a randomized placebo-controlled pilot trial in 25 healthy adults aged 70 to 95. Daily low-dose rapamycin for at least 8 weeks was generally well tolerated, with small changes in red blood cell measures and no rise in blood glucose or insulin resistance. The trial was short and small. PubMed lists her, in the seventh author position, at the Department of Microbiology, Immunology, and Molecular Genetics, UT Health San Antonio. Her name also appears on a 2012 mouse paper (MAJ2012), but PubMed gives no affiliation for her there, so it was not counted.

highlights.KRA2018: Seventh author on the pilot trial testing the safety of rapamycin in older adults.

Kraig E.lab_name: Barshop Institute for Longevity and Aging Studies, The University of Texas Health Science Center (San Antonio, Texas, USA)
Kraig E.role: First author of a 2018 randomized pilot trial of rapamycin safety in healthy older adults.
Kraig E.sub: Barshop Institute for Longevity and Aging Studies, and Department of Cell Systems and Anatomy, The University of Texas Health Science Center, San Antonio
story: Ellen Kraig is first author of an Atlas study (KRA2018), a randomized placebo-controlled pilot trial in 25 healthy adults aged 70 to 95. Daily low-dose rapamycin for at least 8 weeks was generally well tolerated, with small changes in red blood cell measures and no rise in blood glucose or insulin resistance. The trial was short and small. PubMed lists Kraig at the Barshop Institute and the Department of Cell Systems and Anatomy, UT Health San Antonio. Her name also appears on a 2012 mouse paper (MAJ2012), but PubMed gives no affiliation for her there, so it was not counted.

highlights.KRA2018: First author: reported the pilot trial of rapamycin safety, immune markers, physical performance and cognition in older adults.

Musi N.lab_name: Barshop Institute for Longevity and Aging Studies, The University of Texas Health Science Center (San Antonio, Texas, USA)
Musi N.role: Co-author of a 2018 randomized pilot trial of rapamycin safety in healthy older adults.
Musi N.sub: Barshop Institute for Longevity and Aging Studies, and Department of Medicine, The University of Texas Health Science Center, San Antonio
story: Nicolas Musi is a co-author of an Atlas study (KRA2018), a randomized placebo-controlled pilot trial in 25 healthy adults aged 70 to 95. Daily low-dose rapamycin for at least 8 weeks was generally well tolerated, with small changes in red blood cell measures and no rise in blood glucose or insulin resistance. The trial was short and small. PubMed lists Musi, in the tenth author position, at the Barshop Institute and the Department of Medicine, UT Health San Antonio, and at the South Texas Veterans Health Care System. A 2001 metformin paper in the Atlas (ZHO2001) lists only the initial N, so it was not counted.

highlights.KRA2018: Tenth author on the pilot trial testing the safety of rapamycin in older adults.

Kristiansen JB.lab_name: Exercise Biology, Department of Public Health, Aarhus University (Aarhus, Denmark)
Kristiansen JB.role: First author of a 2026 ex vivo mouse muscle study on mTORC1 and JNK-SMAD2L responses to stretch in young and old muscle.
Kristiansen JB.sub: Exercise Biology, Department of Public Health, Aarhus University, Denmark
story: Jonas Boritz Kristiansen is first author of an Atlas study (KRISTIANSEN2026) on muscle from adult and 24-month-old female mice, kept alive outside the body. A standard passive stretch raised mTORC1 signaling to a similar degree in both age groups. The JNK-SMAD2L response to the same stretch was weaker in old muscle. The authors read this as mTORC1 mechanosensing being preserved with age in this model. PubMed lists Kristiansen at Aarhus University.

highlights.KRISTIANSEN2026: First author: reported that stretch-induced mTORC1 signaling is preserved in old mouse muscle while JNK-SMAD2L signaling is blunted.

Kusuda T.lab_name: Department of Allergy and Rheumatology, Graduate School of Medicine, The University of Tokyo (Tokyo, Japan)
Kusuda T.role: First author of a 2026 study on CASTOR1, an arginine sensor that restrains mTORC1 in B cells, and lupus-like disease in mice.
Kusuda T.sub: Department of Allergy and Rheumatology, University of Tokyo (PubMed affiliation, 2026)
story: Takeshi Kusuda was first author of a 2026 Atlas study from the University of Tokyo (KUS2026). It gave the arginine sensor CASTOR1 a clear job upstream of mTORC1. Mice without it had more active mTORC1 in B cells, more antibody-making plasma cells, and lupus-like kidney damage.
