In people with lupus, lower CASTOR1 in plasmablasts went with higher disease activity.

highlights.KUS2026: First author; PubMed lists the author in the Department of Allergy and Rheumatology at the University of Tokyo.

Laberge RM.lab_name: Buck Institute for Research on Aging (Novato, California, USA)
Laberge RM.role: First author of a 2015 study showing that mTOR drives the inflammatory secretions of senescent cells by boosting IL1A translation.
Laberge RM.sub: Buck Institute for Research on Aging (PubMed affiliation, 2015)
story: Remi-Martin Laberge was first author of a 2015 Nature Cell Biology paper in the Atlas (LAB2015), written at the Buck Institute with 20 co-authors. Old, non-dividing (senescent) cells release inflammatory signals called the SASP. The study found that mTOR switches on the production of IL1A, a cytokine near the top of that cascade, and that rapamycin shuts this down. In mice, rapamycin also stopped senescent cells from helping prostate tumours grow.

highlights.LAB2015: First author of the cell and mouse study linking mTOR, IL1A translation and the senescence secretory profile.

Lane CM.lab_name: Department of Cardiovascular Diseases, Mayo Clinic (Rochester, Minnesota, USA)
Lane CM.role: First author of a 2026 trial of low-dose rapamycin in frail older adults with heart failure with preserved ejection fraction.
Lane CM.sub: Department of Cardiovascular Diseases, Mayo Clinic (PubMed affiliation, 2026)
story: Conor M Lane was first author of a 2026 Mayo Clinic Proceedings paper in the Atlas (LAN2026). It tested low-dose rapamycin in frail older adults who have heart failure with preserved ejection fraction. The team included groups at Mayo Clinic and the University of Wisconsin-Madison. The abstract was not yet available when the Atlas entry was made, so results are not summarised here.

highlights.LAN2026: First author; PubMed lists the author in the Department of Cardiovascular Diseases at Mayo Clinic.

Landoas A.lab_name: Pharmacy Department, Grenoble Alpes University Hospital (Grenoble, France)
Landoas A.role: First author of a 2026 retrospective study of everolimus timing and chronic lung allograft dysfunction in lung transplant patients.
Landoas A.sub: Pharmacy Department, Grenoble Alpes University Hospital (PubMed affiliation, 2026)
story: Agathe Landoas was first author of a 2026 study from Grenoble Alpes University Hospital (LANDOAS2026). It looked back at lung transplant patients who received everolimus, an mTOR inhibitor. Starting everolimus later, and stopping and restarting it more often, went with a higher risk of chronic lung allograft dysfunction. This was a single-centre review of records, so it cannot show cause and effect.

highlights.LANDOAS2026: First author; PubMed lists the author in the Pharmacy Department of Grenoble Alpes University Hospital.

Morita M.lab_name: Department of Biochemistry, McGill University (Montreal, Quebec, Canada)
Morita M.role: First author of a 2013 study showing that mTORC1 controls mitochondrial activity through 4E-BP-dependent translation.
Morita M.sub: Department of Biochemistry and Goodman Cancer Research Centre, McGill University (PubMed affiliation, 2013)
story: Masahiro Morita was first author of a 2013 Cell Metabolism paper from McGill University (MOR2013). The study found that mTORC1 helps cells build and run mitochondria by turning up the translation of mitochondria-related messenger RNAs, through the 4E-BP proteins. PubMed also lists a Masahiro Morita as second author of a 2012 metformin paper in the Atlas (LAR2012), but that record has no affiliation, so it is not counted here.

highlights.MOR2013: First author; PubMed lists the author in the Department of Biochemistry and the Goodman Cancer Research Centre at McGill University.

Hakkola J.lab_name: Research Unit of Biomedicine and Internal Medicine, Pharmacology and Toxicology, University of Oulu (Oulu, Finland)
Hakkola J.role: Senior (last) author of a 2026 study of PXR-driven liver growth in healthy volunteers and mice, with AKT-MTOR activation in male mice.
Hakkola J.sub: Pharmacology and Toxicology, Research Unit of Biomedicine and Internal Medicine, University of Oulu (PubMed affiliation, 2026)
story: Jukka Hakkola was last author of a 2026 study from the University of Oulu (LASSILA2026). In 16 healthy volunteers, one week of rifampicin raised the liver-to-body-weight ratio by 2.7 percent. In male mice, activating the same receptor (PXR) enlarged the liver and raised AKT-MTOR activity, without the YAP activation seen in earlier work. PubMed places the group at the Oulu research unit.

highlights.LASSILA2026: Last author; PubMed lists the author in the Research Unit of Biomedicine and Internal Medicine at the University of Oulu.

Lassila P.lab_name: Research Unit of Biomedicine and Internal Medicine, Pharmacology and Toxicology, University of Oulu (Oulu, Finland)
Lassila P.role: First author of a 2026 study of PXR-driven liver growth in healthy volunteers and mice, with AKT-MTOR activation in male mice.
Lassila P.sub: Pharmacology and Toxicology, Research Unit of Biomedicine and Internal Medicine, University of Oulu (PubMed affiliation, 2026)
story: Piia Lassila was first author of a 2026 study from the University of Oulu (LASSILA2026). In 16 healthy volunteers, one week of rifampicin raised the liver-to-body-weight ratio by 2.7 percent. In male mice, activating the receptor PXR enlarged the liver and raised AKT-MTOR activity, but not YAP activity.

highlights.LASSILA2026: First author; PubMed lists the author in the Research Unit of Biomedicine and Internal Medicine at the University of Oulu.

Kim DJ.lab_name: Department of Molecular and Cell Biology, University of California, Berkeley (Berkeley, California, USA)
Kim DJ.role: Co-author of three structural and cell-biology studies of the Rag GTPase-Ragulator system that recruits mTORC1 to the lysosome.
Kim DJ.sub: Department of Molecular and Cell Biology, University of California, Berkeley (PubMed affiliation, 2017–2019)
story: Do Jin Kim appears as a middle author on three Atlas papers from Berkeley, all about how mTORC1 is brought to the lysosome. In 2017 the group solved the structure of the Ragulator complex bound to the Rag proteins (SUX2017). In 2018 they showed that nutrients loosen the Rag-Ragulator grip so the Rags cycle on and off (LAW2018). In 2019 they published the structure of the folliculin complex, which acts as a checkpoint on Rag activation (LAW2019).
PubMed lists the author in the Department of Molecular and Cell Biology at the University of California, Berkeley, on all three papers.

highlights.SUX2017: Middle author of the Ragulator-RagA/C structure paper.
highlights.LAW2018: Middle author of the study of the nutrient-controlled Rag-Ragulator affinity switch.
highlights.LAW2019: Middle author of the folliculin-Rag cryo-EM structure paper.

Lim CY.lab_name: Department of Molecular and Cell Biology, University of California, Berkeley (Berkeley, California, USA)
Lim CY.role: Co-author of two Berkeley studies, on the folliculin-Rag checkpoint (2019) and the LYCHOS cholesterol sensor (2022).
Lim CY.sub: Department of Molecular and Cell Biology, University of California, Berkeley (PubMed affiliation, 2019–2022)
story: Chun-Yan Lim is a middle author on two Atlas papers from the Berkeley group. The 2019 paper gave the structure of the lysosomal folliculin complex, a checkpoint that holds back Rag activation of mTORC1 (LAW2019). The 2022 paper found LYCHOS, a lysosomal protein that senses cholesterol and passes the signal to mTORC1 by sequestering the GATOR1 complex (SHI2022).
PubMed lists the author in the Department of Molecular and Cell Biology at the University of California, Berkeley, on both.

highlights.LAW2019: Middle author of the folliculin-Rag cryo-EM structure paper.
highlights.SHI2022: Middle author of the study that identified LYCHOS as a cholesterol sensor for mTORC1.

Lee JH.lab_name: Laboratory of Gene Regulation and Signal Transduction, Department of Pharmacology, School of Medicine, University of California San Diego (La Jolla, California, USA)
Lee JH.role: First author of a 2010 fruit fly study of Sestrin as a feedback inhibitor of TOR that guards against age-related damage.
Lee JH.sub: Department of Pharmacology, University of California San Diego School of Medicine (PubMed affiliation, 2010)
story: Jun Hee Lee was first author of a 2010 Science paper in the Atlas (LEE2010), listed at the University of California San Diego. In fruit flies, Sestrin rises when TOR stays active, and then pushes TOR back down. Flies without Sestrin built up fat and developed mitochondrial, muscle and heart problems that looked like ageing. Blocking TOR or switching on AMPK prevented these problems.

highlights.LEE2010: First author of the fruit fly study on Sestrin and TOR feedback.

Lee DJW.lab_name: Healthy Longevity Translational Research Program, Yong Loo Lin School of Medicine, National University of Singapore (Singapore)
Lee DJW.role: First author of a 2024 systematic review of rapamycin and its derivatives for ageing-related changes in humans.
Lee DJW.sub: Healthy Longevity Translational Research Program, National University of Singapore (PubMed affiliation, 2024)
story: Deborah J W Lee was first author of a 2024 Lancet Healthy Longevity systematic review in the Atlas (LEE2024), with two co-authors. The team searched five databases and found 18,400 papers, of which 19 studies were included. Rapamycin and related drugs improved some immune, heart and skin measures, with no clear effect on hormones, muscle or the nervous system. Infections and blood fats rose in people who already had age-related disease.

highlights.LEE2024: First author of the systematic review; PubMed lists the author at the National University of Singapore.

Lee SY.lab_name: Center for Vascular Research, Institute for Basic Science (Daejeon, South Korea)
Lee SY.role: First author of a 2026 mouse study showing that ectopic ERBB4 in excitatory neurons drives Alzheimer's-like changes through mTOR signalling.
Lee SY.sub: Center for Vascular Research, Institute for Basic Science, and KAIST (PubMed affiliation, 2026)
story: Se Young Lee was first author of a 2026 Nature paper in the Atlas (LEE2026), with 12 co-authors from IBS, KAIST and UNIST in Korea. In Alzheimer's disease mice, excitatory neurons switched on the gene Erbb4 early. Removing it protected against synapse loss, plaques and memory problems, and adding it to normal mice reproduced most of the damage, though not the plaques. These effects needed mTOR signalling downstream of ERBB4.

highlights.LEE2026: First author; PubMed lists the author at the Center for Vascular Research of the Institute for Basic Science and in the Department of Biological Sciences at KAIST.

Lei HT.lab_name: Janelia Research Campus, Howard Hughes Medical Institute (Ashburn, Virginia, USA)
Lei HT.role: First author of a 2018 crystal structure of arginine-bound SLC38A9, the lysosomal arginine transporter linked to mTORC1.
Lei HT.sub: Janelia Research Campus, Howard Hughes Medical Institute (PubMed affiliation, 2018)
story: Hsiang-Ting Lei was first author of a 2018 paper in Nature Structural and Molecular Biology (LEI2018), with three co-authors. The team solved the crystal structure of zebrafish SLC38A9 holding an arginine molecule. SLC38A9 sits on the lysosome and helps tell mTORC1 which amino acids are available, so the structure shows how that binding works.

highlights.LEI2018: First author of the SLC38A9 arginine crystal structure; PubMed lists the work at the Janelia Research Campus.

Lelegren M.lab_name: Barshop Institute for Longevity and Aging Studies, University of Texas Health Science Center at San Antonio (San Antonio, Texas, USA)
Lelegren M.role: First author of a 2016 study of how rapamycin changes protein-quality-control systems in marmoset liver, muscle and fat.
Lelegren M.sub: Barshop Institute, University of Texas Health Science Center at San Antonio (PubMed affiliation, 2016)
story: Matthew Lelegren was first author of a 2016 paper on marmosets treated with rapamycin (LEL2016), from the Barshop Institute in San Antonio. In liver and muscle, rapamycin went with more of a core proteasome subunit, although proteasome activity did not change. Helper proteins in mitochondria rose in muscle but not liver, and autophagy rose in muscle and fat but not liver. The effects depended on the tissue.

highlights.LEL2016: First author; PubMed lists the author at the South Texas Veterans Health Care System and the Barshop Institute.

Ross C.lab_name: Barshop Institute for Longevity and Aging Studies, University of Texas Health Science Center at San Antonio (San Antonio, Texas, USA)
Ross C.role: Author of three marmoset rapamycin studies: first author of the 2015 metabolic study and co-author of the 2014 and 2016 papers.
Ross C.sub: Barshop Institute, University of Texas Health Science Center at San Antonio; Texas A&M University San Antonio (PubMed affiliation, 2014–2016)
story: Corinna Ross was first author of the 2015 Atlas study of long-term rapamycin in common marmosets (ROS2015). Body weight, activity, blood fats and glucose handling barely changed, so the metabolic side effects were small. Ross is also a co-author of the 2014 paper that first described dosing and blood levels of rapamycin in marmosets (TAR2014), and of the 2016 paper on proteasome and autophagy changes in the same animals (LEL2016).
PubMed lists the author at the Barshop Institute in San Antonio on all three, and at Texas A&M University San Antonio on the first two.

highlights.ROS2015: First author of the study of metabolic effects of long-term rapamycin in marmosets.
highlights.TAR2014: Second author of the paper that first described rapamycin dosing in marmosets.
highlights.LEL2016: Middle author of the marmoset proteostasis study.

Tardif S.lab_name: Barshop Institute for Longevity and Aging Studies, University of Texas Health Science Center at San Antonio (San Antonio, Texas, USA)
Tardif S.role: First author of the 2014 marmoset rapamycin dosing study and senior author of the 2015 marmoset metabolic study, plus co-author of a 2016 follow-up.
Tardif S.sub: Barshop Institute, University of Texas Health Science Center at San Antonio; Southwest National Primate Research Center (PubMed affiliation, 2014–2016)
story: Suzette Tardif was first author of the 2014 Atlas paper that first described how to dose rapamycin in the common marmoset (TAR2014). Oral rapamycin reached blood levels like those used in mouse and human work, and it lowered mTORC1 signalling in tissues. Tardif was last author of the 2015 follow-up, which found only minor metabolic effects of long-term treatment (ROS2015), and is a co-author of the 2016 study on proteasome and autophagy changes (LEL2016).
PubMed lists the author at the Barshop Institute in San Antonio and at the Southwest National Primate Research Center on these papers.

highlights.TAR2014: First author of the marmoset rapamycin dosing and tolerability study.
highlights.ROS2015: Last author of the study of metabolic effects of long-term rapamycin in marmosets.
highlights.LEL2016: Co-author of the marmoset proteostasis study.

Wang Zhenhai.lab_name: Neurology Center, General Hospital of Ningxia Medical University (Yinchuan, Ningxia, China)
Wang Zhenhai.role: Senior (last) author of a 2026 cell study on Brucella suis strain 2, macrophage polarisation, autophagy and PI3K/Akt/mTOR signalling.
Wang Zhenhai.sub: Neurology Center, General Hospital of Ningxia Medical University (PubMed affiliation, 2026)
story: Zhenhai Wang was last author of a 2026 study in the Journal of Medical Microbiology (LI2026B), written with four co-authors in Ningxia, China. In cultured BV2 microglia-like cells, the vaccine strain Brucella suis S2 pushed cells into a mixed M1/M2 state and switched on autophagy. The M2 state and autophagy together helped the bacteria multiply inside cells, through PI3K/Akt/mTOR signalling. This was cell work, not an animal or human study.

highlights.LI2026B: Last author; PubMed lists the author at the Neurology Center and the Institute of Medical Sciences of the General Hospital of Ningxia Medical University.

Liang X.lab_name: Department of Environmental Health, School of Public Health, Shanxi Medical University (Taiyuan, Shanxi, China)
Liang X.role: First author of a 2026 study of how the lncRNA LINP1 binds mTOR and limits radiation-induced senescence in skin cells.
Liang X.sub: Department of Environmental Health, School of Public Health, Shanxi Medical University (PubMed affiliation, 2026)
story: Xiaoting Liang was first author of a 2026 study in Molecular and Cellular Biochemistry (LIANG2026). The long non-coding RNA LINP1 rises after radiation and binds the FAT domain of mTOR. That weakens the contact between mTOR and p53, so less p53 is phosphorylated and fewer skin cells turn senescent. The team tested keratinocytes and human skin samples kept in the lab.

highlights.LIANG2026: First author; PubMed lists the author at Shanxi Medical University, Taiyuan.

Li N.lab_name: Laboratory of Molecular Psychiatry, Department of Psychiatry, Yale University School of Medicine (New Haven, Connecticut, USA)
Li N.role: First author of a 2010 rat study showing that ketamine's fast antidepressant effects need mTOR-dependent synapse formation.
Li N.sub: Department of Psychiatry, Yale University School of Medicine (PubMed affiliation, 2010)
story: Nanxin Li was first author of a 2010 Science paper in the Atlas (LIX2010), from the Yale psychiatry group. In rats, ketamine quickly switched on mTOR in the prefrontal cortex and led to new synaptic spines. Blocking mTOR with rapamycin stopped both the new synapses and the antidepressant-like behaviour. This was animal work, and it points to a mechanism rather than proving the same steps in depressed patients.

highlights.LIX2010: First author of the rat study linking ketamine, mTOR and synapse formation.

Okazaki H.role: First author of a 2013 mouse study on the circadian clock and mTOR in kidney cancer.
Okazaki H.sub: Graduate School of Pharmaceutical Sciences · Kyushu University, Fukuoka, Japan
story: In mice with kidney tumours, active mTOR and total mTOR protein rose and fell over 24 hours. The body clock set this rhythm through the ubiquitin ligase Fbxw7. Giving the mTOR inhibitor everolimus when mTOR was high improved survival, so the time of day of dosing changed the result. Okazaki is the first of ten authors, and PubMed lists Kyushu University.

highlights.OKA2013: First of ten authors on the mouse study showing that everolimus works better when given at the time of day when mTOR is high.

Okazaki H.lab_name: Departments of Pharmaceutics and Pharmaceutical Oncology, Graduate School of Pharmaceutical Sciences, Kyushu University (Fukuoka, Japan)

Oki T.role: First author of a 2021 mouse study imaging mTORC1 activity in acute myeloid leukemia.
Oki T.sub: Center for Regenerative Medicine · Massachusetts General Hospital, Boston, USA
story: Using fluorescent probes in the bone marrow of living mice, the study followed mTORC1 activity in leukemia cells. Activity fell as the disease advanced but was high at the moment of the best response to chemotherapy, where it was switched on rather than selected for. Blocking mTORC1 at that point killed more leukemia cells. Oki is the first of twelve authors, and PubMed lists the Center for Regenerative Medicine at Massachusetts General Hospital.

highlights.OKI2021: First of twelve authors on the mouse imaging study of mTORC1 timing in acute myeloid leukemia.

Oki T.lab_name: Center for Regenerative Medicine, Massachusetts General Hospital (Boston, Massachusetts, USA)

O'Reilly KE.role: First author of a 2006 study showing that mTOR inhibition switches on Akt signalling.
O'Reilly KE.sub: Program in Molecular Pharmacy and Chemistry · Memorial Sloan-Kettering Cancer Center, New York, USA
story: Blocking mTOR removes a feedback brake and turns up signalling through receptor tyrosine kinases, PI3K and Akt. The authors saw Akt activation in cancer cell lines and also in patient tumours treated with everolimus (RAD001), so part of the evidence comes from people. O'Reilly is the first of twelve authors, and PubMed lists Memorial Sloan-Kettering Cancer Center.

highlights.ORE2006: First of twelve authors on the study showing that mTOR inhibition activates Akt, in cell lines and in patient tumours.

O'Reilly KE.lab_name: Program in Molecular Pharmacy and Chemistry, Memorial Sloan-Kettering Cancer Center (New York, New York, USA)

Panchaud N.role: First author of a 2013 yeast study on a GAP complex that turns off TORC1 when amino acids run out.
Panchaud N.sub: Division of Biochemistry, Department of Biology · University of Fribourg, Switzerland
story: In baker's yeast, the Iml1 complex (with Npr2 and Npr3) acts as a GTPase-activating protein for the Rag-family protein Gtr1. When amino acids are missing, it switches Gtr1 off and so lowers TORC1 activity. The authors suggest the matching human proteins may help hold back tumours. Panchaud is the first of three authors, and PubMed lists the University of Fribourg.

highlights.PAN2013: First of three authors on the yeast study of the Iml1 GAP complex acting on Gtr1.

Panchaud N.lab_name: Division of Biochemistry, Department of Biology, University of Fribourg (Fribourg, Switzerland)

Park JM.role: First author of a 2023 cell study redefining how AMPK affects autophagy.
Park JM.sub: Department of Biochemistry, Molecular Biology and Biophysics · University of Minnesota, Minneapolis, USA
story: In cultured cells, AMPK turned out to restrain ULK1 and autophagy during glucose starvation or mitochondrial energy stress, the opposite of the usual textbook picture. AMPK also protected the ULK1 machinery from being broken down by caspases, so cells could restart autophagy later. Park is the first of three authors, and PubMed lists the University of Minnesota.

highlights.PAR2023: First of three authors on the cell study showing that AMPK inhibits ULK1 and autophagy under energy stress.

Park JM.lab_name: Department of Biochemistry, Molecular Biology and Biophysics, University of Minnesota (Minneapolis, Minnesota, USA)

Paul D.role: First author of a 2025 study on how mTOR briefly switches off APC/C to boost glycolysis at cell cycle entry.
Paul D.sub: Laboratory of Cancer Biology and Genetics · National Cancer Institute, Bethesda, USA
story: After a growth signal, mTOR quickly adds a phosphate to the APC/C helper protein CDH1, which partly releases it and briefly inactivates APC/C. The glycolysis enzyme PFKFB3 then builds up and glycolysis rises, until a later phosphatase restores APC/C. The pulse of glycolysis is needed for cells to enter the cell cycle. Paul is the first of thirteen authors, and PubMed lists the National Cancer Institute in Bethesda.

highlights.PAU2025: First of thirteen authors on the Nature paper on transient APC/C inactivation by mTOR.

Paul D.lab_name: Laboratory of Cancer Biology and Genetics, Center for Cancer Research, National Cancer Institute (Bethesda, Maryland, USA)

Peng M.role: First author of a 2017 study showing that SZT2 organizes the GATOR complexes that control mTORC1.
Peng M.sub: Immunology Program · Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, New York, USA
story: The study, in cells and mice, found that SZT2 pulls GATOR1 and GATOR2 together into one complex that sits on the lysosome and sets how mTORC1 responds to nutrients. Cells lacking SZT2 kept mTORC1 on even when starved, and SZT2-deficient newborn mice died. Peng is the first of three authors, and PubMed lists the Immunology Program at Memorial Sloan Kettering.

highlights.PEN2017: First of three authors on the study showing that SZT2 organizes GATOR control of mTORC1.

Peng M.lab_name: Immunology Program, Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center (New York, New York, USA)

Perez K.role: First author of a 2026 methods study on a cross-species platform for screening lifespan-extending drugs.
story: The team built a high-throughput platform that tests compounds for effects on lifespan in yeast, worms, flies, killifish and mice, using automated imaging and deep-learning death detection. More than 400 compounds were tested, and the results pointed to drugs that act in several species and to longevity pathways shared across them. This is a methods and screening study. Perez is the first of eleven authors, and PubMed lists EPITERNA in Épalinges, with other institutions in Switzerland also named.

highlights.PEREZ2026: First of eleven authors on the cross-species lifespan drug-screening platform.

Petit CS.role: First author of a 2013 study on folliculin and the lysosome-based activation of mTORC1.
Petit CS.sub: Department of Cell Biology · Yale University School of Medicine, New Haven, USA
story: In human cells, folliculin (FLCN, the protein behind Birt-Hogg-Dube syndrome) gathers on lysosomes when amino acids are removed and binds RagA directly. FLCN is needed for amino acids to bring mTORC1 to the lysosome through the Rag proteins. Petit is the first of three authors, and PubMed lists the Department of Cell Biology at Yale. Petit is also listed on a 2012 TFEB paper in the Atlas, but that record carries no affiliation, so it is not counted here.

highlights.PET2013: First of three authors on the study of folliculin recruitment to lysosomes and Rag GTPase activation.

Petit CS.lab_name: Department of Cell Biology, Yale University School of Medicine (New Haven, Connecticut, USA)

Roczniak-Ferguson A.role: First author of a 2012 study showing that mTORC1 phosphorylates TFEB to control lysosome genes.
Roczniak-Ferguson A.sub: Department of Cell Biology · Yale University School of Medicine, New Haven, USA
story: In human cells, mTORC1 on the lysosome adds a phosphate to TFEB at serine 211, which lets 14-3-3 proteins hold TFEB in the cytoplasm. When lysosome function is blocked, TFEB loses the phosphate and moves into the nucleus, where it switches on lysosome and autophagy genes. Roczniak-Ferguson is the first of eight authors, and PubMed lists the Department of Cell Biology at Yale. A 2013 Atlas paper carries the same given name but no affiliation, so it is not counted here.

highlights.ROC2012: First of eight authors on the study showing that mTORC1 phosphorylates TFEB to control lysosome gene activity.

Roczniak-Ferguson A.lab_name: Department of Cell Biology, Yale University School of Medicine (New Haven, Connecticut, USA)

Pledger ES.role: First author of a 2026 study on translation of 5' TOP mRNAs in chronically activated human CD8+ T cells.
Pledger ES.sub: Department of Molecular and Cell Biology · University of California Berkeley, USA
story: Using ribosome profiling in human CD8+ T cells grown in the lab, the study found that 5' TOP mRNAs were translated much less during chronic activation, a model of T cell exhaustion. This happened even though mTOR activity looked high, so the repression is not explained by lower mTOR signalling. Pledger is the first of four authors, and PubMed lists the Department of Molecular and Cell Biology at UC Berkeley.

highlights.PLEDGER2026: First of four authors on the ribosome profiling study of 5' TOP mRNA repression in chronically activated CD8+ T cells.

Pledger ES.lab_name: Department of Molecular and Cell Biology, University of California Berkeley (Berkeley, California, USA)

Porstmann T.role: First author of a 2008 study showing that mTORC1 controls SREBP and lipid synthesis downstream of Akt.
Porstmann T.sub: Gene Expression Analysis Laboratory · London, UK
story: In cells and in fruit flies, Akt-driven lipid synthesis needed mTORC1. Rapamycin stopped the mature form of the transcription factor SREBP1 from building up in the nucleus and lowered its target genes. Silencing SREBP blocked Akt-driven fat synthesis and reduced cell size. Porstmann is the first of nine authors, and PubMed lists the Gene Expression Analysis Laboratory in London without naming a larger institution.

highlights.POR2008: First of nine authors on the study showing that mTORC1 regulates SREBP and lipogenesis in Akt-dependent growth.

Poulsen MM.role: First author of a 2012 randomized trial of high-dose resveratrol in obese men.
Poulsen MM.sub: Department of Endocrinology and Internal Medicine · Aarhus University Hospital, Denmark
story: In this randomized, placebo-controlled trial, 24 obese but otherwise healthy men took high-dose resveratrol or placebo for four weeks. Resveratrol did not improve insulin sensitivity, blood pressure or body composition, which does not match the promising results from rodents. Poulsen is the first of ten authors, and PubMed lists Aarhus University Hospital.

highlights.POU2013: First of ten authors on the placebo-controlled trial of resveratrol in obese men.

Poulsen MM.lab_name: Department of Endocrinology and Internal Medicine, Aarhus University Hospital (Aarhus, Denmark)

Pyo JO.role: First author of a 2013 mouse study showing that extra Atg5 raises autophagy and lifespan.
Pyo JO.sub: School of Biological Sciences/Bio-MAX Institute · Seoul National University, Korea
story: Mice engineered to carry extra copies of the autophagy gene Atg5 lived about 17 percent longer at the median. They were leaner and more sensitive to insulin, and cells from them resisted oxidative damage better. Pyo is the first of eight authors, and PubMed lists the Global Research Laboratory at Seoul National University.

highlights.PYO2013: First of eight authors on the mouse study of Atg5 overexpression and lifespan.

Pyo JO.lab_name: Global Research Laboratory, School of Biological Sciences/Bio-MAX Institute, Seoul National University (Seoul, South Korea)

Ramanathan C.role: First author of a 2018 study showing that mTOR sets the speed and strength of circadian clocks.
Ramanathan C.sub: Department of Biological Sciences · University of Memphis, USA
story: Blocking mTOR made circadian clocks run slower and flatter, and activating it made them run faster and stronger. This was seen in cultured cells, in brain (SCN) and liver tissue taken from mice, and in mice with one copy of the mTOR gene, whose activity rhythm ran longer. Ramanathan is the first of eight authors, and PubMed lists the University of Memphis.

highlights.RAM2018: First of eight authors on the study of mTOR and circadian clock period and amplitude.

Ramanathan C.lab_name: Department of Biological Sciences, University of Memphis (Memphis, Tennessee, USA)

Feng X.role: Last author of a 2026 study on SLC7A5, mTOR, autophagy and cisplatin tolerance.
Feng X.sub: State Key Laboratory of Oral Diseases · West China Hospital of Stomatology, Sichuan University, Chengdu, China
story: In a genome-wide CRISPR screen of cancer cells, blocking mTOR made cells more tolerant to cisplatin by switching on protective autophagy, the opposite of the usual view. The amino acid transporter SLC7A5 sits at the centre of this circuit, and adding leucine made SLC7A5-expressing tumour cells more sensitive to cisplatin. Feng is the last of seven authors, and PubMed lists the West China Hospital of Stomatology at Sichuan University.

highlights.RAO2026: Last of seven authors on the CRISPR screen study of SLC7A5, mTOR-autophagy signalling and cisplatin tolerance.

Feng X.lab_name: State Key Laboratory of Oral Diseases, West China Hospital of Stomatology, Sichuan University (Chengdu, Sichuan, China)

Rao P.role: First author of a 2026 study on SLC7A5, mTOR, autophagy and cisplatin tolerance.
Rao P.sub: State Key Laboratory of Oral Diseases · West China Hospital of Stomatology, Sichuan University, Chengdu, China
story: In a genome-wide CRISPR screen of cancer cells, blocking mTOR made cells more tolerant to cisplatin by switching on protective autophagy, the opposite of the usual view. The amino acid transporter SLC7A5 sits at the centre of this circuit, and adding leucine made SLC7A5-expressing tumour cells more sensitive to cisplatin. Rao is the first of seven authors, and PubMed lists the West China Hospital of Stomatology at Sichuan University.

highlights.RAO2026: First of seven authors on the CRISPR screen study of SLC7A5, mTOR-autophagy signalling and cisplatin tolerance.

Rao P.lab_name: State Key Laboratory of Oral Diseases, West China Hospital of Stomatology, Sichuan University (Chengdu, Sichuan, China)

Rauch B.role: First author of a 2026 cell study on tankyrases, AMPK, mTOR and fat cell differentiation.
Rauch B.sub: Department of Medical Chemistry, Faculty of Medicine · University of Debrecen, Hungary
story: Deleting tankyrase 1 or 2 slowed the maturation of fat cells in a cell line, with less autophagy, more AMPK activity and weaker mTORC1 activity. The slow differentiation in TNKS2-knockout cells was rescued by activating autophagy or by blocking LKB1, and TNKS2 was found to add ADP-ribose to LKB1. Rauch is the first of eight authors, and PubMed lists the Department of Medical Chemistry at the University of Debrecen.

highlights.RAUCH2026: First of eight authors on the study of tankyrase-2, AMPK and mTOR in fat cell differentiation.

Rauch B.lab_name: Department of Medical Chemistry, Faculty of Medicine, University of Debrecen (Debrecen, Hungary)

Rebsamen M.role: First author of a 2015 study identifying SLC38A9 as part of the lysosomal amino acid sensing machinery for mTORC1.
Rebsamen M.sub: CeMM Research Center for Molecular Medicine · Austrian Academy of Sciences, Vienna, Austria
story: In human cells, SLC38A9, a transporter in the lysosome membrane, was found to be part of the Ragulator-Rag machinery. Cells with extra SLC38A9 resisted amino acid withdrawal, and cells without it activated mTORC1 poorly in response to amino acids. Rebsamen is the first of twenty authors, and PubMed lists CeMM in Vienna.

highlights.REB2015: First of twenty authors on the paper identifying SLC38A9 as a component of the amino acid sensing machinery controlling mTORC1.

Rebsamen M.lab_name: CeMM Research Center for Molecular Medicine of the Austrian Academy of Sciences (Vienna, Austria)

Ren Y.role: First author of a 2026 study on a gut-tumour bacterium, kynurenic acid and resistance to PD-1 blockade in gastric cancer.
Ren Y.sub: Department of General Surgery, Nanfang Hospital · Southern Medical University, Guangzhou, China
story: Using patient tissue and mouse models, the study linked the bacterium Streptococcus anginosus to resistance to PD-1 immunotherapy in gastric cancer. Its product kynurenic acid raised ITGA2 and dampened an mTOR-dependent chain that supports CD8+ T cell killing. Blocking ITGA2 restored T-cell activity in the models. Ren is the first of ten authors, and PubMed lists the Department of General Surgery at Nanfang Hospital.

highlights.REN2026: First of ten authors on the study of kynurenic acid, the ITGA2-mTOR-CTSV axis and PD-1 resistance in gastric cancer.

Ren Y.lab_name: Department of General Surgery, Nanfang Hospital, Southern Medical University (Guangzhou, China)

Robida-Stubbs S.role: First author of a 2012 study of TOR signalling, rapamycin and lifespan in worms through SKN-1 and DAF-16.
Robida-Stubbs S.sub: Joslin Diabetes Center · Harvard Medical School, Boston, USA
story: In the worm C. elegans, blocking TORC1 genetically extended lifespan through SKN-1/Nrf and DAF-16/FoxO. Rapamycin also extended lifespan, but only through SKN-1 and not DAF-16, probably because it also affects TORC2. Rapamycin triggered a similar protective response in mice. Robida-Stubbs is the first of eight authors, and PubMed lists the Joslin Diabetes Center and Harvard Medical School.

highlights.ROB2012: First of eight authors on the worm study of TOR, rapamycin and lifespan through SKN-1 and DAF-16.

Shimobayashi M.role: First author of a review on the mTOR network in metabolism and signalling crosstalk, and middle author of two other Atlas studies, an mTORC2 structure and a phosphoproteomics study.
story: Mitsugu Shimobayashi was first author of a 2014 review in the Atlas, written with Michael N. Hall, on how the mTOR network connects to metabolism and to other signalling pathways. PubMed lists the author at the Biozentrum of the University of Basel.

The author is also a middle author on two research papers. One is the 2020 cryo-EM structure of human mTORC2 at 3.2 angstrom resolution, which points to the C-terminal end of Rictor as the reason this complex does not respond to rapamycin. The other is a 2013 phosphoproteomics study showing that mTORC1 switches on de novo pyrimidine synthesis.

highlights.SHI2014: First author of the review on the mTOR network in metabolism and signalling crosstalk.
highlights.SCA2020: Middle author of the cryo-EM structure of human mTORC2, listed at the Biozentrum, University of Basel.
highlights.ROB2013: Middle author of the phosphoproteomics study showing that mTORC1 activates de novo pyrimidine synthesis.

Brignole EJ.lab_name: Department of Biology, Massachusetts Institute of Technology (Cambridge, Massachusetts, USA)
Brignole EJ.role: Middle author of three cryo-EM structure papers on the nutrient-sensing machinery upstream of mTORC1: GATOR1, Raptor with Rag-Ragulator, and GATOR2.
Brignole EJ.sub: Department of Biology and MIT.nano, Massachusetts Institute of Technology
story: Edward J. Brignole is a middle author on three structural papers in the Atlas, all with David M. Sabatini as senior author. PubMed lists the author at the Department of Biology of the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and at MIT.nano.

The 2018 paper gives cryo-EM structures of GATOR1, alone and bound to the Rag GTPases. The 2019 paper shows how Raptor docks onto Rag-Ragulator, so that mTORC1 can reach the lysosome. The 2022 paper gives the structure of human GATOR2, a large cage-like complex; the study notes that how GATOR2 inhibits GATOR1 is still not fully settled. All three are structures of purified proteins, not studies in animals or people.

highlights.VAL2022: Middle author of the cryo-EM structure of the human GATOR2 complex.
highlights.ROG2019: Middle author of the structure of Raptor bound to Rag-Ragulator, showing how mTORC1 docks on the lysosome.
highlights.SHE2018: Middle author of the cryo-EM structures of GATOR1 and GATOR1-Rag GTPase complexes.

Kraus WE.lab_name: Duke Clinical Research Institute, Duke University School of Medicine (Durham, North Carolina, USA)
Kraus WE.role: Co-author, listed as the last named author, of the two-year caloric restriction safety trial in healthy non-obese adults.
Kraus WE.sub: Duke Clinical Research Institute and Duke University School of Medicine
story: William E. Kraus is the last named author of a randomized multicentre trial in the Atlas that tested whether two years of 25% caloric restriction is safe in healthy adults who are not obese. PubMed lists the author at the Duke Clinical Research Institute and Duke University School of Medicine. PubMed's author list ends with a blank entry after this name.
The trial found that the diet was safe overall, but bone mineral density fell more in the restriction group than in the control group.

highlights.ROM2016: Last named author of the trial of two-year caloric restriction in healthy non-obese adults.

Romashkan SV.lab_name: National Institute on Aging (Bethesda, Maryland, USA)
Romashkan SV.role: First author of the two-year caloric restriction safety trial in healthy non-obese adults.
Romashkan SV.sub: National Institute on Aging, Bethesda, Maryland
story: Sergei V. Romashkan was first author of a randomized multicentre trial in the Atlas on two years of 25% caloric restriction in healthy adults who were not obese. PubMed lists the author at the National Institute on Aging in Bethesda.
The trial found the diet safe and well tolerated overall, with one finding to watch: bone mineral density dropped more in the restriction group than in controls.

highlights.ROM2016: First author of the trial of two-year caloric restriction in healthy non-obese adults.

Ruvinsky I.lab_name: Department of Biochemistry, The Hebrew University-Hadassah Medical School (Jerusalem, Israel)
Ruvinsky I.role: First author of the 2005 knock-in mouse study showing that ribosomal protein S6 phosphorylation sets cell size and glucose handling.
Ruvinsky I.sub: Department of Biochemistry, The Hebrew University-Hadassah Medical School, Jerusalem, Israel
story: Igor Ruvinsky was first author of a 2005 mouse study in the Atlas, with Oded Meyuhas as last author. PubMed lists the author at the Hebrew University-Hadassah Medical School in Jerusalem. The team made knock-in mice in which all five phosphorylatable serines of ribosomal protein S6 were changed to alanine, so S6 could not be phosphorylated.

Contrary to the model of the time, the mutation did not change the translation of 5'TOP mRNAs. Cells from these mice made protein faster and divided faster, yet were smaller, and rapamycin did not shrink them further. Pancreatic beta cells were also small, and the adult mice had low insulin and impaired glucose tolerance.

highlights.RUV2005: First author: made S6 phosphorylation-deficient knock-in mice and showed the cells and beta cells were small, with impaired glucose tolerance.

Saci A.lab_name: Division of Signal Transduction, Department of Medicine, Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center, Harvard Medical School (Boston, Massachusetts, USA)
Saci A.role: First author of the 2011 study showing that Rac1 regulates mTORC1 and mTORC2 and controls cell size.
Saci A.sub: Division of Signal Transduction, Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center, Harvard Medical School
story: Abdelhafid Saci was first author of a 2011 study in the Atlas, with Lewis C. Cantley and Christopher L. Carpenter, on the small GTPase Rac1. PubMed lists the author at the Division of Signal Transduction, Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center, Harvard Medical School.

The work, done in cultured cells, found that Rac1 binds mTOR and helps place mTORC1 and mTORC2 at specific membranes. Deleting Rac1 in primary cells lowered the activity of both complexes and affected cell size.

highlights.SAC2011: First author: showed that Rac1 binds and regulates both mTORC1 and mTORC2 in cells.

Sang Z.lab_name: Department of Chemistry, Southern University of Science and Technology (Shenzhen, China)
Sang Z.role: First author of the 2026 chemical-proteomics study identifying PKM2 as a methionine sensor for mTORC1.
Sang Z.sub: Department of Chemistry, Southern University of Science and Technology, Shenzhen, and Hong Kong Baptist University
story: Zixin Sang was first author of a 2026 paper in the Atlas that asks how cells sense the amino acid methionine. PubMed lists the author at the Department of Chemistry of the Southern University of Science and Technology in Shenzhen and at Hong Kong Baptist University.

The team built a methionine analogue that can be locked onto the proteins that grab it inside living cells. With it they found that the enzyme PKM2 binds methionine in a separate pocket, not through its usual enzyme activity, and passes the signal to mTORC1 through the GATOR2 complex. This was cell work, not a study in animals or people.

highlights.SANG2026: First author: developed the methionine probe and identified PKM2 as a methionine sensor acting through GATOR2.

Saucedo LJ.lab_name: Division of Basic Sciences, Fred Hutchinson Cancer Research Center (Seattle, Washington, USA)
Saucedo LJ.role: First author of the 2003 fruit fly study showing that Rheb promotes cell growth in the insulin/TOR network.
Saucedo LJ.sub: Division of Basic Sciences, Fred Hutchinson Cancer Research Center, Seattle, Washington
story: Leslie J. Saucedo was first author of a 2003 study in the Atlas, with Bruce A. Edgar as last author. PubMed lists the author at the Division of Basic Sciences of the Fred Hutchinson Cancer Research Center in Seattle.

The team screened fruit flies (Drosophila) for new regulators of growth and found Rheb. More Rheb made cells grow, and losing it stopped larval growth. Genetic tests placed Rheb downstream of Tsc1-Tsc2 and upstream of TOR. This was work in flies.

highlights.SAU2003: First author: identified Rheb in a Drosophila screen and placed it between Tsc1-Tsc2 and TOR.

Knockenhauer KE.lab_name: Department of Biology, Massachusetts Institute of Technology (Cambridge, Massachusetts, USA)
Knockenhauer KE.role: Middle author of two structure papers on amino acid sensors upstream of mTORC1, CASTOR1 for arginine and Sestrin2 for leucine.
Knockenhauer KE.sub: Department of Biology, Massachusetts Institute of Technology
story: Kevin E. Knockenhauer is a middle author on two structural papers in the Atlas from the group of David M. Sabatini. PubMed lists the author at the Department of Biology of the Massachusetts Institute of Technology on the 2015 paper.

The 2015 paper solved the crystal structure of Sestrin2 bound to leucine and showed the pocket that lets it act as a leucine sensor for mTORC1. The 2016 paper solved the structure of CASTOR1 bound to arginine and showed how arginine binding releases CASTOR1 from GATOR2. Both are structures of purified proteins.

highlights.SAX2016: Middle author of the crystal structure of arginine-bound CASTOR1.
highlights.SAX2015: Middle author of the crystal structure of Sestrin2 bound to leucine.

Schwartz TU.lab_name: Department of Biology, Massachusetts Institute of Technology (Cambridge, Massachusetts, USA)
Schwartz TU.role: Middle author of two structure papers on amino acid sensors upstream of mTORC1, CASTOR1 for arginine and Sestrin2 for leucine.
Schwartz TU.sub: Department of Biology, Massachusetts Institute of Technology
story: Thomas U. Schwartz is a middle author on two structural papers in the Atlas on how mTORC1 senses amino acids. PubMed lists the author at the Department of Biology of the Massachusetts Institute of Technology on the 2015 paper.

The 2015 paper gives the crystal structure of Sestrin2 holding leucine. The 2016 paper gives the structure of CASTOR1 holding arginine. Both are structures of purified proteins, backed by tests in cells.

highlights.SAX2016: Fourth of five authors on the crystal structure of arginine-bound CASTOR1.
highlights.SAX2015: Middle author of the crystal structure of Sestrin2 bound to leucine.

Saxena A.lab_name: Division of Cancer and Genetics, School of Medicine, Cardiff University (Cardiff, United Kingdom)
Saxena A.role: First author of the 2026 TRON randomised trial of everolimus for neuropsychological problems in tuberous sclerosis complex.
Saxena A.sub: Division of Cancer and Genetics, School of Medicine, Cardiff University, UK
story: Anurag Saxena was first author of the 2026 TRON trial in the Atlas, with Julian R. Sampson as last author. PubMed lists the author at the Division of Cancer and Genetics, School of Medicine, Cardiff University.

The multicentre trial randomised 38 people with tuberous sclerosis complex, two to one, to everolimus or placebo for 24 weeks. Similar shares of people improved on thinking tests with the drug and with placebo (87% and 75%), which points to strong practice or placebo effects rather than a clear benefit for cognition.

highlights.SAX2026: First author of the randomised trial of everolimus for neuropsychological deficits in tuberous sclerosis complex.

Scaiola A.lab_name: Institute for Molecular Biology and Biophysics, ETH Zurich (Zurich, Switzerland)
Scaiola A.role: First author of the 3.2 angstrom mTORC2 structure and middle author of the earlier mTORC2 core complex architecture paper.
Scaiola A.sub: Institute for Molecular Biology and Biophysics, ETH Zurich
story: Alain Scaiola was first author of the 2020 cryo-EM structure of human mTORC2 in the Atlas, with Timm Maier and Nenad Ban as senior authors. PubMed lists the author at the Institute for Molecular Biology and Biophysics at ETH Zurich. The structure, at 3.2 angstrom resolution, points to the C-terminal part of Rictor as the source of the complex's resistance to rapamycin.
He is also a middle author on the 2018 paper that gave the first architecture of the human mTORC2 core complex (mTOR, Rictor, SIN1 and mLST8) from the same two research groups.

highlights.SCA2020: First author of the 3.2 angstrom cryo-EM structure of human mTORC2.
highlights.STU2018: Middle author of the architecture of the human mTORC2 core complex.

Stuttfeld E.role: First author of the 2018 architecture of the human mTORC2 core complex and middle author of the 2020 mTORC2 structure.
story: Edward Stuttfeld was first author of the 2018 eLife paper in the Atlas that reported the architecture of the human mTORC2 core complex, made of mTOR, Rictor, SIN1 and mLST8. PubMed lists the author at the Biozentrum of the University of Basel. The structure helped explain why mTORC2 is insensitive to rapamycin.
The author is also a middle author on the 2020 follow-up, a 3.2 angstrom cryo-EM structure of human mTORC2 that points to the C-terminus of Rictor as the source of that insensitivity.

highlights.STU2018: First author of the architecture of the human mTORC2 core complex.
highlights.SCA2020: Middle author of the 3.2 angstrom cryo-EM structure of human mTORC2.

Schalm SS.lab_name: Department of Cell Biology, Harvard Medical School (Boston, Massachusetts, USA)
Schalm SS.role: First author of the 2003 study showing that the TOS motif lets raptor bind 4E-BP1 and control its phosphorylation.
Schalm SS.sub: Department of Cell Biology, Harvard Medical School
story: Stefanie S. Schalm was first author of a 2003 study in the Atlas, with John Blenis as last author and David M. Sabatini among the authors. PubMed lists the author at the Department of Cell Biology at Harvard Medical School.

The work, done in cells and in test tubes, showed that a short stretch called the TOS motif lets 4E-BP1 bind raptor, so that mTOR can phosphorylate it at several sites and 4E-BP1 lets go of the translation factor eIF4E.

highlights.SCH2003: First author: showed that the TOS motif mediates raptor binding and multisite phosphorylation of 4E-BP1.

Schram AM.lab_name: Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center (New York, New York, USA)
Schram AM.role: First author of the first-in-human phase 1 trial of the mTORC1-selective inhibitor RMC-5552.
Schram AM.sub: Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, New York
story: Alison M. Schram was first author of the 2025 phase 1 trial in the Atlas of RMC-5552, a drug built to block mTORC1 more than mTORC2. PubMed lists the author at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center in New York.

The trial gave escalating weekly doses to 57 people with advanced solid tumours. High blood sugar, a side effect of older mTOR drugs, occurred in 4% of patients, and 64% had disease control. There was no comparison group and no head-to-head test against rapamycin, so this is early evidence.

highlights.SCH2025: First author of the phase 1 trial of RMC-5552 in advanced solid tumours.

Sciarretta S.lab_name: Cardiovascular Research Institute, Rutgers New Jersey Medical School (Newark, New Jersey, USA)
Sciarretta S.role: First author of a 2014 review of mTOR signalling in cardiac physiology and disease.
Sciarretta S.sub: Cardiovascular Research Institute, Rutgers New Jersey Medical School, and IRCCS Neuromed, Pozzilli, Italy
story: Sebastiano Sciarretta was first author of a 2014 review in the Atlas, written with Massimo Volpe and Junichi Sadoshima, on what mTOR does in the healthy and the diseased heart. PubMed lists the author at the Cardiovascular Research Institute, Rutgers New Jersey Medical School, and at IRCCS Neuromed in Pozzilli, Italy.
The review pulls together findings on how mTORC1 supports the heart and how partial blocking of it may protect against some forms of heart damage.

highlights.SCI2014: First author of the review of mTOR signalling in cardiac physiology and disease.

Shah OJ.lab_name: Molecular and Cellular Biology Laboratory, Salk Institute for Biological Studies (La Jolla, California, USA)
Shah OJ.role: First author of the 2004 study showing that constant TSC/Rheb/mTOR/S6K activity depletes IRS1 and IRS2 and causes insulin resistance in cells.
Shah OJ.sub: Molecular and Cellular Biology Laboratory, Salk Institute for Biological Studies
story: O. Jameel Shah was first author of a 2004 study in the Atlas, with Tony Hunter as last author. PubMed lists the author at the Molecular and Cellular Biology Laboratory of the Salk Institute for Biological Studies in La Jolla.

In cultured mammalian cells, constant activity of the Rheb/mTOR/S6K chain lowered the levels of IRS1 and IRS2, which made the cells resistant to insulin and weakened their survival signals. The paper is the companion to a second study that together set out the S6K1 to IRS feedback loop.

highlights.SHA2004: First author: showed in cells that constitutive Rheb/mTOR/S6K activity depletes IRS1 and IRS2 and causes insulin resistance.

Huang RK.lab_name: Howard Hughes Medical Institute, Janelia Research Campus (Ashburn, Virginia, USA)
Huang RK.role: Middle author of two cryo-EM papers on Rag GTPase regulators, GATOR1 and FLCN-FNIP2.
Huang RK.sub: Howard Hughes Medical Institute, Janelia Research Campus
story: Rick K. Huang is a middle author on two cryo-EM papers in the Atlas on how the Rag GTPases, which pass nutrient signals to mTORC1, are regulated. PubMed lists the author at the Howard Hughes Medical Institute, Janelia Research Campus, in Virginia.

The 2018 paper gives structures of GATOR1 and of GATOR1 bound to the Rag GTPases. The 2019 paper gives the structure of the FLCN-FNIP2 complex bound to the Rags and Ragulator. Both are structures of purified human proteins, tested with biochemical assays.

highlights.SHE2019: Middle author of the cryo-EM structure of the human FLCN-FNIP2-Rag-Ragulator complex.
highlights.SHE2018: Middle author of the cryo-EM structures of GATOR1 and GATOR1-Rag GTPase complexes.

Shin HR.lab_name: Department of Molecular and Cell Biology, University of California, Berkeley (Berkeley, California, USA)
Shin HR.role: First author of the 2022 study identifying LYCHOS as a lysosomal cholesterol sensor for mTORC1.
Shin HR.sub: Department of Molecular and Cell Biology, University of California, Berkeley
story: Hijai R. Shin was first author of the 2022 Science paper in the Atlas, with Roberto Zoncu as last author. PubMed lists the author at the Department of Molecular and Cell Biology of the University of California, Berkeley.

The team found that a lysosomal protein called LYCHOS binds cholesterol. When cholesterol is high, LYCHOS holds on to the GATOR1 complex, which frees mTORC1 to move to the lysosome and switch on. Changing the cholesterol-binding site weakened mTORC1 activation. The work was done in cells.

highlights.SHI2022: First author: identified LYCHOS as a cholesterol sensor that connects to GATOR1 and mTORC1 at the lysosome.

Shim JH.lab_name: Department of Anatomy, Korea University College of Medicine (Seoul, Republic of Korea)
Shim JH.role: First author of the 2026 study of the D-leucine prodrug DLMEH, which activates mTORC1 through Sestrin2 in muscle atrophy models.
Shim JH.sub: Department of Anatomy, Korea University College of Medicine, Seoul
story: Jae Ho Shim was first author of a 2026 paper in the Atlas on DLMEH, a modified D-leucine compound. PubMed lists the author at the Department of Anatomy of the Korea University College of Medicine in Seoul.

DLMEH bound Sestrin2 about as strongly as L-leucine and switched on mTORC1 in a Sestrin2-dependent way. It restored protein synthesis in human muscle cells and kept muscle mass, grip strength and endurance in rats with drug-induced muscle wasting. That rat model is not an ageing model of sarcopenia.

highlights.SHIM2026: First author of the study of DLMEH as a Sestrin2-dependent mTORC1 activator in muscle cells and rats.

Shimada H.lab_name: Department of Obstetrics and Gynecology, University of Colorado Anschutz (Aurora, Colorado, USA)
Shimada H.role: First author of the 2026 study of sex differences in placental mTORC1 signalling, amino acid transport and mitochondrial respiration.
Shimada H.sub: Department of Obstetrics and Gynecology, University of Colorado Anschutz, and Sapporo Medical University
story: Hiroshi Shimada was first author of a 2026 paper in the Atlas with Thomas Jansson and Fredrick J. Rosario among the senior authors. PubMed lists the author at the University of Colorado Anschutz and at Sapporo Medical University in Japan.

The team compared 46 placentas from uncomplicated term pregnancies. Male placentas showed stronger mTORC1 signalling, more System A amino acid transport and higher mitochondrial respiration than female ones. This is an observation at one time point, so it shows an association, not a cause.

highlights.SHIMADA2026: First author of the study comparing mTORC1 signalling and metabolism in male and female term placentas.

Sills AM.lab_name: The Sam and Ann Barshop Institute for Longevity and Aging Studies, UT Health San Antonio (San Antonio, Texas, USA)
Sills AM.role: First author of the 2018 study of long-term rapamycin and blood markers in middle-aged marmosets.
Sills AM.sub: Barshop Institute for Longevity and Aging Studies, UT Health San Antonio
story: Aubrey M. Sills was first author of a 2018 paper in the Atlas, with Adam B. Salmon as last author. PubMed lists the author at the Barshop Institute for Longevity and Aging Studies at UT Health San Antonio.

Middle-aged common marmosets got daily rapamycin. After nine months their blood cell counts changed only a little. Females had lower rapamycin levels in blood than males, yet both sexes changed little, so blood side effects look unlikely in healthy middle-aged animals of this kind.

highlights.SIL2018: First author of the marmoset study of long-term rapamycin and hematological markers.

Sillito F.lab_name: Cancer Institute, University College London (London, United Kingdom)
Sillito F.role: First author of the 2026 study of enforced mTORC1 activity through RHEB in therapeutic CD4+ T cells.
story: Francesca Sillito was first author of a 2026 paper in the Atlas, with Ronjon Chakraverty as last author. PubMed lists the author at the Cancer Institute of University College London.

In mouse CD4+ T cells, extra RHEB raised mTORC1 activity and first boosted growth. After transfer into mice, the cells lasted longer but fought tumours worse, because they became exhausted. The study warns that CD4+ and CD8+ T cells can react differently to the same change.

highlights.SIL2026: First author of the study of RHEB overexpression and exhaustion in CD4+ T cells.

Sinclair LV.lab_name: Division of Cell Signalling and Immunology, University of Dundee (Dundee, United Kingdom)
Sinclair LV.role: First author of the 2013 study showing that antigen receptors control amino acid uptake through Slc7a5 in T cells.
Sinclair LV.sub: Division of Cell Signalling and Immunology, University of Dundee
story: Linda V. Sinclair was first author of a 2013 study in the Atlas, with Doreen A. Cantrell as last author. PubMed lists the author at the Division of Cell Signalling and Immunology of the University of Dundee.

In mouse T cells, activation through the antigen receptor turns up the amino acid transporter Slc7a5. Without it the cells could not take up leucine, mTORC1 and c-Myc stayed low, and the cells did not expand or mature into effector cells.

highlights.SIN2013: First author: showed that Slc7a5-driven amino acid uptake controls mTORC1 and T cell differentiation.

Singh S.lab_name: Lysosomal Health in Ageing, South Australian Health and Medical Research Institute (Adelaide, South Australia, Australia)
Singh S.role: First author of the 2026 randomized crossover trial of reduced dietary protein and autophagy in human blood.
Singh S.sub: Lysosomal Health in Ageing, South Australian Health and Medical Research Institute, and Adelaide University
story: Sanjna Singh was first author of a 2026 trial in the Atlas, with Timothy J. Sargeant as a senior author. PubMed lists the author with the Lysosomal Health in Ageing group at the South Australian Health and Medical Research Institute and at Adelaide University.

In a randomized crossover trial, 63 healthy adults ate a normal-protein diet and a reduced-protein diet for four weeks each. Autophagic flux in blood cells did not differ between the diets, even though animal work had suggested that less protein should raise autophagy.

highlights.SIN2026: First author of the crossover trial of reduced protein intake and autophagic flux in healthy adults.

Simpson SJ.lab_name: Charles Perkins Centre, The University of Sydney (Sydney, New South Wales, Australia)
Simpson SJ.role: Senior author of the 2014 mouse study showing that the protein-to-carbohydrate ratio, not calories, shapes lifespan and metabolic health.
Simpson SJ.sub: Charles Perkins Centre and School of Biological Sciences, The University of Sydney
story: Stephen J. Simpson was last author of a 2014 mouse study in the Atlas, with Samantha M. Solon-Biet as first author. PubMed lists the author at the Charles Perkins Centre and the School of Biological Sciences of The University of Sydney.

Mice were fed many diets that varied in protein, fat and carbohydrate. Lifespan and metabolic health tracked the ratio of protein to carbohydrate, not total calories, and a low protein ratio went with lower mTOR activation in the liver.

highlights.SOL2014: Last author of the study linking the protein-to-carbohydrate ratio to lifespan, metabolic health and liver mTOR activation in mice.

Sinclair DA.lab_name: Department of Genetics, Harvard Medical School (Boston, Massachusetts, USA)
Sinclair DA.role: Middle author of two Atlas studies on lifespan, a mouse diet-ratio study and a multi-site test of five longevity compounds.
Sinclair DA.sub: Department of Genetics, Harvard Medical School, and School of Medical Sciences, University of New South Wales
story: David A. Sinclair is a middle author on two lifespan studies in the Atlas. On the 2014 paper PubMed lists the author at the Department of Genetics, Harvard Medical School, and at the University of New South Wales in Sydney. On the 2012 paper PubMed gives no affiliation for the author.

The 2014 mouse study found that the protein-to-carbohydrate ratio of the diet, not calories, set lifespan and metabolic health. The 2012 study tested resveratrol, green tea extract, curcumin, oxaloacetic acid and medium-chain triglyceride oil in mice and found no significant effect on lifespan for any of them.

highlights.SOL2014: Middle author of the mouse study linking the protein-to-carbohydrate ratio to lifespan and metabolic health.
highlights.STR2012: Middle author of the multi-site test of five compounds, none of which changed lifespan significantly.

Solon-Biet SM.lab_name: Charles Perkins Centre, The University of Sydney (Sydney, New South Wales, Australia)
Solon-Biet SM.role: First author of the 2014 mouse study showing that the protein-to-carbohydrate ratio, not calories, shapes lifespan and metabolic health.
Solon-Biet SM.sub: Charles Perkins Centre, Centre for Education and Research on Aging and ANZAC Research Institute, The University of Sydney
story: Samantha M. Solon-Biet was first author of a 2014 mouse study in the Atlas, with Stephen J. Simpson as last author. PubMed lists the author at the Charles Perkins Centre and Concord Hospital sites of The University of Sydney.

Mice were fed many diets that varied in protein, fat and carbohydrate. Lifespan and metabolic health followed the protein-to-carbohydrate ratio rather than calories, and a low protein ratio went with lower mTOR activation in the liver.

highlights.SOL2014: First author of the study linking the protein-to-carbohydrate ratio to lifespan and metabolic health in mice.

Sparta B.lab_name: Department of Molecular and Cellular Biology, University of California, Davis (Davis, California, USA)
Sparta B.role: First author of the 2023 live-cell imaging study of the mTORC1-TFEB axis.
Sparta B.sub: Department of Molecular and Cellular Biology, University of California, Davis
story: Breanne Sparta was first author of a 2023 paper in the Atlas, with John G. Albeck among the authors. PubMed lists the author at the Department of Molecular and Cellular Biology of the University of California, Davis.

The team followed single human breast-line cells (MCF10A) under the microscope. mTORC1 and TFEB signalling adjusted continuously to amino acids and insulin, and at normal amino acid levels TFEB, AMPK and AKT activity rose and fell together. These changes tracked how fast cells made protein.

highlights.SPA2023: First author of the live-imaging study of continuous nutrient and growth factor sensing by mTORC1-TFEB.

Spilman P.lab_name: Department of Physiology, University of Texas Health Science Center at San Antonio (San Antonio, Texas, USA)
Spilman P.role: First author of the 2010 study showing that rapamycin prevented memory deficits and lowered amyloid-beta in an Alzheimer's mouse model.
Spilman P.sub: Department of Physiology, University of Texas Health Science Center at San Antonio
story: Patricia Spilman was first author of a 2010 mouse study in the Atlas, with Veronica Galvan as last author. PubMed lists the author at the Department of Physiology of the University of Texas Health Science Center at San Antonio.
In mice built to model Alzheimer's disease, long-term rapamycin prevented memory problems and lowered amyloid-beta. The benefit went along with more autophagy in neurons.

highlights.SPI2010: First author: showed that rapamycin prevented cognitive deficits and lowered amyloid-beta in an Alzheimer's mouse model.

Grewal SS.lab_name: Department of Biochemistry and Molecular Biology, Cumming School of Medicine, University of Calgary (Calgary, Alberta, Canada)
Grewal SS.role: Senior author of the 2026 fruit fly study linking nutrient/TOR signalling to mitochondrial TFAM in the fat body.
Grewal SS.sub: Department of Biochemistry and Molecular Biology, Cumming School of Medicine, University of Calgary
story: Savraj S. Grewal was last author of a 2026 paper in the Atlas, with Shrivani Sriskanthadevan-Pirahas as first author. PubMed lists the author at the Cumming School of Medicine of the University of Calgary.

In fruit fly (Drosophila) larvae, nutrient/TOR signalling in the fat body holds down the mitochondrial protein TFAM after transcription. This TOR to TFAM link in the fat body helps set how fast the whole animal grows.

highlights.SRI2026: Last author of the Drosophila study of nutrient/TOR control of fat body TFAM and body growth.

Sriskanthadevan-Pirahas S.lab_name: Department of Biochemistry and Molecular Biology, Cumming School of Medicine, University of Calgary (Calgary, Alberta, Canada)
Sriskanthadevan-Pirahas S.role: First author of the 2026 fruit fly study linking nutrient/TOR signalling to mitochondrial TFAM in the fat body.
Sriskanthadevan-Pirahas S.sub: Department of Biochemistry and Molecular Biology, Cumming School of Medicine, University of Calgary
story: Shrivani Sriskanthadevan-Pirahas was first author of a 2026 paper in the Atlas, with Savraj S. Grewal as last author. PubMed lists the author at the Cumming School of Medicine of the University of Calgary.

In fruit fly (Drosophila) larvae, nutrient/TOR signalling in the fat body holds down the mitochondrial protein TFAM after transcription. This TOR to TFAM link in the fat body helps set how fast the whole animal grows.

highlights.SRI2026: First author of the Drosophila study of nutrient/TOR control of fat body TFAM and body growth.

Su Y.lab_name: Department of Cardiology, Tianjin Medical University (Tianjin, China)
Su Y.role: First author of the 2026 mouse and cell study of lncRNA DLX6-AS1, PI3K/AKT/mTOR and necroptosis after heart ischemia-reperfusion.
Su Y.sub: Department of Cardiology, Tianjin Medical University, and Cangzhou People's Hospital
story: Yanhong Su was first author of a 2026 paper in the Atlas, with Jun Zhang as last author. PubMed lists the author at the Department of Cardiology of Tianjin Medical University and at Cangzhou People's Hospital.

In mice with heart injury after blocked and restored blood flow, and in rat heart cells, the RNA molecule DLX6-AS1 switched on PI3K/AKT/mTOR signalling and promoted necroptosis, a form of cell death. Blocking DLX6-AS1 reduced the cell death and damage.

highlights.SU2026: First author of the study of DLX6-AS1, PI3K/AKT/mTOR and necroptosis in heart ischemia-reperfusion injury.

Zhang Jun.lab_name: Department of Cardiology, Tianjin Medical University (Tianjin, China)
Zhang Jun.role: Senior author of the 2026 mouse and cell study of lncRNA DLX6-AS1, PI3K/AKT/mTOR and necroptosis after heart ischemia-reperfusion.
Zhang Jun.sub: Department of Cardiology, Tianjin Medical University, and Cangzhou Central Hospital
story: Jun Zhang was last author of a 2026 paper in the Atlas, with Yanhong Su as first author. PubMed lists the author at the Department of Cardiology of Tianjin Medical University and at Cangzhou Central Hospital. Zhang is a very common name, so this profile rests on the affiliation on this one paper.

In mice with heart injury after blocked and restored blood flow, and in rat heart cells, the RNA molecule DLX6-AS1 switched on PI3K/AKT/mTOR signalling and promoted necroptosis, a form of cell death. Blocking DLX6-AS1 reduced the cell death and damage.

highlights.SU2026: Last author of the study of DLX6-AS1, PI3K/AKT/mTOR and necroptosis in heart ischemia-reperfusion injury.

Sun Z.lab_name: Department of Hematology, The First Affiliated Hospital of Zhejiang Chinese Medical University (Hangzhou, Zhejiang, China)
Sun Z.role: First author of the 2026 retrospective study of second-line sirolimus in acquired pure red cell aplasia.
Sun Z.sub: Department of Hematology, The First Affiliated Hospital of Zhejiang Chinese Medical University
story: Zexing Sun was first author of a 2026 paper in the Atlas. PubMed lists the author at the Department of Hematology of the First Affiliated Hospital of Zhejiang Chinese Medical University in Hangzhou.

The single-centre review looked back at people with acquired pure red cell aplasia, a disease where the bone marrow stops making red cells. Second-line sirolimus gave a 54.5% response rate, and response did not depend on mutation status. There was no randomisation and no control arm, and the figures for ciclosporin come from different lines of treatment.

highlights.SUN2026: First author of the retrospective study of second-line sirolimus in acquired pure red cell aplasia.

Su MY.lab_name: Department of Molecular and Cell Biology, University of California, Berkeley (Berkeley, California, USA)
Su MY.role: First author of the 2017 hybrid structure of the RagA/C-Ragulator mTORC1 activation complex.
Su MY.sub: Department of Molecular and Cell Biology, University of California, Berkeley
story: Ming-Yuan Su was first author of a 2017 structural paper in the Atlas from the groups of James H. Hurley and Roberto Zoncu. PubMed lists the author at the Department of Molecular and Cell Biology and the California Institute for Quantitative Biosciences at the University of California, Berkeley.
The team solved the crystal structure of the five-part Ragulator complex and used electron microscopy to model how it presents the RagA/C pair, which recruits mTORC1 to the lysosome.

highlights.SUX2017: First author of the hybrid structure of the RagA/C-Ragulator complex.

Suzuki C.lab_name: Department of Biological Chemistry and Molecular Pharmacology, Harvard Medical School (Boston, Massachusetts, USA)
Suzuki C.role: First author of the 2008 study showing how PDCD4 blocks translation initiation by binding eIF4A.
Suzuki C.sub: Department of Biological Chemistry and Molecular Pharmacology, Harvard Medical School
story: Chikako Suzuki was first author of a 2008 study in the Atlas, with Gerhard Wagner as last author. PubMed lists the author at the Department of Biological Chemistry and Molecular Pharmacology at Harvard Medical School.

Using x-ray crystallography, NMR and binding measurements, the team showed that both MA3 domains of PDCD4 bind eIF4A and compete with eIF4G and RNA, which explains how PDCD4 slows the start of translation.

highlights.SUZ2008: First author: solved PDCD4 domain structures and showed both MA3 domains bind eIF4A.

Swarup A.lab_name: Department of Biochemistry and Molecular Biology, University of Georgia (Athens, Georgia, USA)
Swarup A.role: First author of the 2026 yeast study of medulloblastoma-associated DDX3X/Ded1 mutations and the response to TORC1 inhibition.
Swarup A.sub: Department of Biochemistry and Molecular Biology, University of Georgia
story: Akanksha Swarup was first author of a 2026 paper in the Atlas, with Timothy A. Bolger as last author. PubMed lists the author at the Department of Biochemistry and Molecular Biology of the University of Georgia.

The team put cancer-linked DDX3X mutations into the yeast version of the gene, DED1. The mutant yeast grew despite rapamycin and made more protein from mRNAs with simple 5' ends once TORC1 was blocked. This is yeast work, so it suggests a mechanism and does not show it in tumours.

highlights.SWA2026: First author of the yeast study of DDX3X/Ded1 mutations and translation under TORC1 inhibition.

Szwed A.lab_name: Department of Biochemistry and Molecular Biology, Robert Wood Johnson Medical School, Rutgers University (Piscataway, New Jersey, USA)
Szwed A.role: First author of the 2021 review of the regulation and metabolic functions of mTORC1 and mTORC2.
Szwed A.sub: Department of Biochemistry and Molecular Biology, Robert Wood Johnson Medical School, Rutgers University
story: Angelia Szwed was first author of a 2021 review in Physiological Reviews, included in the Atlas, written with Eugene Kim and Estela Jacinto. PubMed lists the author at the Department of Biochemistry and Molecular Biology, Robert Wood Johnson Medical School, Rutgers University.
The review covers how mTORC1 and mTORC2 are controlled and what each does in metabolism, with examples from cancer, immune cells, diabetes and obesity, brain disease and ageing.

highlights.SZW2021: First author of the review on the regulation and metabolic functions of mTORC1 and mTORC2.

Tang B.lab_name: Department of Urology, Institute of Urology, West China Hospital, Sichuan University (Chengdu, China)
Tang B.role: First author of a study on how clear cell kidney cancer resists mTOR inhibitors.
Tang B.sub: Department of Urology, West China Hospital, Sichuan University
story: Bo Tang was first author of the Atlas study TAN2026, which looked at clear cell renal cell carcinoma, a kidney cancer. It describes one way these tumours escape the mTOR inhibitors everolimus and temsirolimus. The protein SPOP adds a K63-linked ubiquitin tag to ZMYND8, which keeps ZMYND8 out of phase-separated compartments in the cell. ZMYND8 can then work with ZHX2 to switch on the NEK7 gene, and p70S6K is activated by another route that does not need mTOR. A drug built to destroy NEK7 restored everolimus sensitivity. PubMed lists Tang at the Department of Urology, West China Hospital, Sichuan University.

highlights.TAN2026: First author: reported that SPOP-driven ubiquitination of ZMYND8 lets kidney cancer cells keep p70S6K active despite mTOR inhibitors.

Tao J.lab_name: Research Centre of Environmental Ecology and Fish Nutrition, College of Fisheries and Life Science, Shanghai Ocean University (Shanghai, China)
Tao J.role: First author of a study of mTOR/SREBP1 signalling and liver glycogen build-up in a carnivorous fish.
Tao J.sub: College of Fisheries and Life Science, Shanghai Ocean University
story: Jiajie Tao was first author of the Atlas study TAO2026, done in a carnivorous fish. In the liver, the insulin-responsive mTOR/SREBP1 pathway helps decide whether glucose is turned into fat or stored as glycogen. In this fish the pathway is impaired, and that goes together with a heavy build-up of liver glycogen that resembles glucose intolerance. This is an animal study, and the finding is an association. PubMed lists Tao at Shanghai Ocean University.

highlights.TAO2026: First author: helped show that weak mTOR/SREBP1 signalling goes with liver glycogen overload in a carnivorous fish.

Li S.lab_name: Research Centre of Environmental Ecology and Fish Nutrition, College of Fisheries and Life Science, Shanghai Ocean University (Shanghai, China)
Li S.role: Last author of a study of mTOR/SREBP1 signalling and liver glycogen build-up in a carnivorous fish.
Li S.sub: College of Fisheries and Life Science, Shanghai Ocean University
story: Songlin Li was last author of the Atlas study TAO2026, done in a carnivorous fish. The paper links the insulin-responsive mTOR/SREBP1 pathway to the choice between making fat and storing glycogen in the liver. When the pathway is impaired in this fish, glycogen piles up in the liver, much like in glucose intolerance. It is an animal study and shows an association. PubMed lists Li at the College of Fisheries and Life Science, Shanghai Ocean University.

highlights.TAO2026: Last author: senior author of the fish study linking impaired mTOR/SREBP1 signalling to liver glycogen overload.

Tiwari A.lab_name: Cancer Genome and Epigenetics Program, Sanford Burnham Prebys Medical Discovery Institute (La Jolla, California, USA)
Tiwari A.role: First author of a study of the circPVT1-encoded micropeptide Firefox and MYC-driven cancer.
Tiwari A.sub: Cancer Genome and Epigenetics Program, Sanford Burnham Prebys Medical Discovery Institute
story: Ashutosh Tiwari was first author of the Atlas study TIW2026 in Genes & Development. It describes a small protein called Firefox (FFX), made from the circular RNA circPVT1. FFX boosts AKT-mTORC1 signalling and cap-dependent translation, which keeps MYC protein levels high. When FFX was removed, MYC levels dropped and tumours grew less in mouse xenograft models of MYC-amplified cancer. PubMed lists Tiwari at the Sanford Burnham Prebys Medical Discovery Institute in La Jolla.

highlights.TIW2026: First author: reported that the micropeptide Firefox sustains AKT-mTORC1 signalling and MYC levels in MYC-driven cancer models.

Bagchi A.lab_name: Cancer Genome and Epigenetics Program, Sanford Burnham Prebys Medical Discovery Institute (La Jolla, California, USA)
Bagchi A.role: Last author of a study of the circPVT1-encoded micropeptide Firefox and MYC-driven cancer.
Bagchi A.sub: Cancer Genome and Epigenetics Program, Sanford Burnham Prebys Medical Discovery Institute
story: Anindya Bagchi was last author of the Atlas study TIW2026 in Genes & Development. The paper shows that Firefox (FFX), a small protein encoded by the circular RNA circPVT1, stimulates AKT-mTORC1 signalling and cap-dependent translation to keep MYC protein abundant. Depleting FFX lowered MYC and slowed tumour growth in xenograft models of MYC-amplified cancer, which points to an mTORC1-linked weak spot in such tumours. PubMed lists Bagchi at the Sanford Burnham Prebys Medical Discovery Institute in La Jolla.

highlights.TIW2026: Last author: senior author of the study showing that Firefox supports MYC through AKT-mTORC1 signalling.

Tsun ZY.lab_name: Whitehead Institute for Biomedical Research and Department of Biology, Massachusetts Institute of Technology (Cambridge, Massachusetts, USA)
Tsun ZY.role: First author of the 2013 folliculin study and co-author of the 2015 SLC38A9 paper, both from the Whitehead Institute.
Tsun ZY.sub: Whitehead Institute for Biomedical Research & Department of Biology, MIT (papers from 2013 and 2015)
story: Zhi-Yang Tsun was first author of the Atlas study TSU2013 in Molecular Cell. Working in cells, the paper showed that the folliculin tumour suppressor, together with FNIP, acts as a GAP (an activating helper) for the RagC and RagD GTPases. Rag proteins carrying GDP are needed to bind mTORC1 and bring it to the lysosome, where amino acids switch it on.
